subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF REAPPOINTMENT OF MR. DONALD GORDON

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF REAPPOINTMENT OF MR. DONALD GORDON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make an announcement regarding the chairmanship of the board of directors of the Canadian National Railways. Mr. Donald Gordon has been today reappointed to that position by an order in council passed pursuant to sections 6 and 8 of the Canadian National Railways Act, and in accordance with an understanding referred to by him in an exchange of correspondence with me, which I would like to read to the house.
My letter to Mr. Gordon is dated October 2, and reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Gordon:
Some time ago, when I discussed with you the question of the expiry of your present appointment on September 30, you indicated that while reluctant to bear any longer than necessary the heavy responsibilities that you have now shouldered for many years, you were also concerned about the completion of certain work to reorganize and strengthen the railway.
The government now invites you to complete that work by accepting reappointment as chairman and director. We believe that this would be not only to the advantage of the railway but also of the country.
In asking you to accept this reappointment to the position which expired last Monday, I wish to express to you the great appreciation of the government for the distinguished and tireless service that you have already given as chairman and president of the Canadian National Railways.
Mr. Gordon's reply to that letter on October 3 is as follows:
My dear Prime Minister:
I have received your letter of October 2 inviting me to continue as chairman of the board of directors of Canadian National Railways.
As you mention in your letter, I am anxious to be relieved, when it is possible, of these heavy
and varied responsibilities which, I have learned, go beyond the field of railway management. I am nevertheless also concerned, as I have already told you, with seeing through to completion the work referred to in your letter.
This work should be finished in about a year and a half, in which case I will, in good conscience, ask to be released from the duties which I have always done my best to perform in a way which would be of benefit to the railway and to the country which I have now had the great honour to serve for many years, in war and in peace.
In accepting reappointment on the understanding above mentioned, I would like to recall the exchange of correspondence we have had on certain unfounded charges, which have distressed me greatly, that I have discriminated against or am unfair to French speaking employees of Canadian National Railways.
In this connection, I would remind you of the evidence I have recently sent you which should dispel any feeling that in Canadian National Railways we do not sufficiently recognize the claims of French speaking Canadians to posts of responsibility or the importance of bilingual qualifications in the holding of such posts.
Yours sincerely,
D. Gordon,
President.
I would be glad to table the order in council, this exchange of correspondence and the evidence which Mr. Gordon refers to in his letter to me, namely the letter he has written to me on the subject of certain charges made against him and a memorandum on that matter.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under standing order 26 I ask leave to move the adjournment of the house in order to discuss a matter of urgent national importance, namely the threat to the flow of grain shipments on the great lakes and the St. Lawrence seaway due to a lack of any effective action being taken by the government of Canada which has had its culmination this morning in the strike of longshoremen in the St. Lawrence river ports.
This is a matter of urgency and national importance. The disruption of grain shipments to the U.S.S.R. which will result will mean serious and possibly irreparable damage to Canada's economy as a whole.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
The hon. member for Ontario, seconded by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, has presented a certain motion asking for leave to adjourn the house under standing order 26 on the grounds of great urgency. May I remind the house that "urgency within this rule", standing order 26, "does not apply to the matter itself, but it means urgency of debate, when the ordinary opportunities provided by the rules of the house do not permit the subject to be brought on early enough and public interest demands that discussion take place immediately". That is Beauchesne, fourth edition, paragraph 3 of citation 100. Also:
The reason for allowing such a motion... is to afford members an opportunity of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance which they could do in no other way.
That is Mr. Speaker Black in the Journals of the house, March 31, 1931, page 50.
The urgency of debate is something that has to be considered. ...In my experience it has never happened in the house that while the speech from the throne was being currently debated a motion for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance under the new standing order 26 was agreed to.

Perhaps that is a little bit off the rails; nevertheless it deals with the same subject. That is Mr. Speaker Beaudoin, Hansard, January 11, 1956, page 20.
On June 27, 1961, as will be found on page 7105 of Hansard, Mr. Speaker Michener expressed a similar view with regard to a motion made under standing order 26 during the budget debate, when he said:
It seems to me that it is a matter which could very readily be debated in the budget debate.
Later on the same page he added:
"I accept the proposition that this is an urgent and important public matter to which the Leader of the Opposition draws attention. It is a definite matter of public importance. However, that is not the criterion in determining whether standing order 26 should be applied. The criterion is whether there is an opportunity to debate this matter in an effective way."
He concluded his remarks on page 7106 by saying:
.. .1 am not satisfied that there is not ample opportunity to put before the house and the government all the considerations that apply to this important matter in the debate which will follow immediately after the calling of the orders of the day.
Therefore he rejected the request of the then leader of the opposition. For similar reasons, in view of the fact that interim supply will follow within half an hour, let us hope, it seems to me there is ample opportunity today to discuss this urgent and important matter. Therefore I do not feel that the motion is in order at this time.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: May I just say a word on a point of order. I realize there is ample opportunity to discuss any matter one wishes on interim supply. Mr. Chairman, I wish to continue my remarks this morning and deal especially with a statement made a while ago by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson).
It is plain that the appointment which the Prime Minister announced this morning constituted a difficult problem for the present government. On the one hand, pressure was brought to bear by the directors of the Canadian National Railways and certain heads of labour movements to maintain the present chairman in office. On the other hand, pressure was also brought to bear to remove him from office or rather not to reappoint him.
In the first place, I want to congratulate the Prime Minister for his courage and his boldness in taking such a decision which was not an easy one in the circumstances.
As far as I am concerned, Mr. Chairman, I had sometime earlier the opportunity to question the chairman of National Railways. It also happens that I in no way agreed with him on certain points, but, personally, I never asked for the head of the present chairman of the C.N.R. I asked him to use his head, but I never wanted to see his head chopped off as chairman.
In the letter he wrote to the Prime Minister, the chairman of National Railways today admits that there is a problem of bilingualism within the C.N.R., and that the representation of French Canadians on the higher levels is inadequate. He does take a step forward when he acknowledges existing conditions, and we have always welcomed repentant sinners with open arms.
If the chairman of National Railways is ready to admit that some errors have been committed in the past, if he is ready to admit, as he has done, that there actually is a problem of biculturalism and bilingualism in that crown corporation, I think he has taken a great step forward and that it would be well to give him a chance to do now what he failed to do in the past.

I think that this is the more important because, thanks to his many years of experience, and following all the pressure put on the National Railways administration, he is better able to see that one should actually reconsider all those things, this whole French fact inside the most important crown corporation, that is, the C.N.R.
I seem to understand that his term of office would be renewed for only a year and a half. However, we are not to be fooled, because it is obvious that those two letters have been written by arrangement and that the whole business was concocted so that the chairman of National Railways would himself put a limit to his term, which would more or less be a compromise suggested and accepted by the chairman now in office of the Canadian National Railways.
We understand perfectly well what is behind all that-a year and a half. The president of the Canadian National Railways will come before the committee, and we will be ready to give him a fond welcome and tell him exactly what we want.
We do not wish to confine ourselves to destructive criticism. We want our criticism to be quite constructive. By criticizing in a practical way, by means of realistic suggestions and positive ideas, we want to help solve the problems which may exist within confederation and not try to stir up the two races one against the other. Instead of that, one race must tell the other what it means by confederation and the other one must try to understand the other's point of view.
Mr. Chairman, in my opinion, that is the only way we can succeed in solving the problems Canada now faces. I believe in confederation, providing we are fully aware of what can happen, that is that French Canadians have to become first class citizens of this country. They want their responsibilities as such and, moreover, they want to be able to say and do by themselves what they want to say and do. And I think that all the civil service and cabinet members know now that the one who is still the most able to ensure the survival of confederation at this time and who carries the heaviest burden is the Minister of Finance since he holds in his hands the ultimatum of the premier of Quebec to the effect that he wants the province to get back 25 per cent of the tax on corporations, 25 per cent of personal income taxes, and 100 per cent of succession duties.
It is a first request but it is the most important and that which comes first place at this time if we really want confederation to survive.
April 5 next will be "D day" for confederation. Will the present government agree to give back to the provinces the sources of
Interim Supply
revenue they are entitled to? I hope so, otherwise I believe that day will see the greatest split within confederation; at that time, we French Canadians will be in a position to say: Well, after all, maybe we are better off alone than in confederation where we are refused our responsibilities and the sources of revenue that would enable us to assume them. Mr. Chairman, that is a determining factor.
The other day, I heard the Prime Minister say on the C.B.C.'s French and English television networks: We agree that the provinces have responsibilities, but the federal government also has its own responsibilities. That is true. But the Prime Minister should seriously tell himself that the present government has assumed responsibilities that did not rightly belong to it.
By entering the fields of highways, education, hospital insurance, etc., the present government has assumed responsibilities which the federal government did not have to assume; and if the federal government had not assumed those responsibilities at that time, it should not have been forced to take away from the provinces sources of revenues which they need. If the provinces had retained their sources of revenues, they could assume their responsibilities in the fields of education, highways, hospital insurance, agriculture, etc. If the federal government has greater responsibilities today, it is because it has entered the provincial field.
During the first part of the session, the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Lamon-tagne) said that where a province wanted to resume its responsibilities in certain fields, there should be no reason why it should not at the same time get back its former sources of revenues.
I am surprised, Mr. Chairman, to note that the government of Quebec has not asked officially to resume those responsibilities, which should be his, as well as the moneys related to them. I hope the provincial government will carry out the suggestion of the President of the Privy Council, that is resume its responsibilities in those fields as well as the sources of revenue to carry out those responsibilities.
Mr. Chairman, I apologize if I am slowly coming near my Liberal colleagues. The reason is that I realize that they need to be convinced. I should not say convinced but indeed persuaded. I know they are convinced of what I said today.

I rise on a point of order, Mr. Chairman. It is not so much the fact that the hon. member for Lapointe is coming nearer to us that concerns us, but the fact

that he is standing in front of the Sergeant-at-Arms while he is speaking, and this is altogether out of order.

There would always be a solution, Mr. Chairman, that is to move the Sergeant-at-Arms.
I can assure you, Mr. Chairman, that these are important factors in confederation-determining factors for the French Canadian race and Quebec Liberals are of the same opinion. I am convinced that it is partisanship that prevents them from saying out loud what they believe down in their hearts, and I hope, Mr. Chairman, that for the greatest benefit of all, they will put aside party considerations.
The Prime Minister himself, the leader of the Liberal party, said on television that partisanship must be put aside in order to solve the great problems facing Canada.
I have a suggestion to make that I did not expect to make this morning, it has to do with the reappointment of the president of the Canadian National Railways. We want to prove that we are without bias, that we are willing to help toward the solution of problems, and that we know what they actually are. They have nothing to do with the appointment of an individual, of a president in particular, but they consist in a group of very definite principles the most important of which is to give back to the provinces their sources of income. There are others, such as a greater participation of French Canadians in the federal public service. After what happened in the past, I am sure that the present C.N.R. president has decided to assume his responsibilities.
Mr. Chairman, before concluding my remarks, I wish to tell you that the present problem raised in the house could easily be settled by recognizing a group of 13 French Canadian members from the province of Quebec who wish to assert without fanaticism but with determination, the French fact within confederation. And now after a week, nothing has been done and it seems that this group of French Canadian members who wish to be recognized are being deliberately ignored.
It rests with certain members of the government to see that a decision is taken as soon as possible, because it is absolutely illogical and utterly ridiculous not to recognize a group of 13 members of the province of Quebec who have been elected with majorities comparable to that of any of your members.
Certain members have formed a political party and wish to assert the French fact within confederation.
Mr. Chairman, I think that the present government must take a decision in this con-

nection, not in a week's time, but immediately. I think that the problem can be solved before the end of the week. The following fact cannot be disregarded: 13 members who wish to emphasize a definite point in this house.

Mr. Chairman, what I intend to do on this occasion is deal with some elements of the question that was raised by my hon. friend the member for Ontario, namely the threat to the flow of grain shipments on the great lakes and the St. Lawrence seaway which, as stated in the motion, we believe is due to lack of any effective action being taken by the government of Canada.
I start by a reference to a statement made by the Minister of Labour this morning when he referred to this matter while answering a question. He stated that, after all, the strike had only been on for three and a half hours. This statement, I feel, may well rank with other classic statements that have been made by ministers throughout the years, not losing sight at the moment of the one, "What's a million dollars, anyhow?". This was a most unusual statement for the minister to make, because he is usually a member who chooses his language with great care. No doubt harried by the experiences of the last few days he made that statement, which taken literally does not show that regard for the seriousness of the situation that should characterize a minister of labour.
I should like also to refer to the statement made by the Prime Minister this morning in relation to the Banks situation. He said, when asked by the hon. member for Three Rivers when the trusteeship legislation would be proceeded with, "When there is no hope of a private settlement". This answer is one that completely disregards the interests of the Canadian people.
The Minister of Labour has reiterated a denial he made to me the other day, that to his knowledge there has been no threat by the S.I.U. to the effect that if there were a possibility of the legislation for trusteeship being proceeded with there would be trouble and a tie-up of shipping on the St. Lawrence. When he says he has not heard that, I naturally accept his statement in that regard. But I would point out that is not the view of others intimately connected with this matter. I would point out that there has been some correspondence between Mr. J. D. Leitch, president of Upper Lakes Shipping Limited, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Labour. This correspondence consists of telegrams one of which is dated, as I am informed, October 1. In the course of that telegram Mr. Leitch has pointed out that while his company has been directly interested

in what is taking place, in the lawlessness on the great lakes, his company has not been consulted at any time. He says this:
Regret that at no point has a representative of our company been consulted.
Then he says this:
It is my firm conviction that as a question of law and order there is no room to compromise... and the Canadian government must give firm leadership and not be deterred by the threats of *waterfront hoodlums.
May I ask the right hon. gentleman from what he is reading?
I am reading from a telegram about which the Prime Minister should know, he having received it from Mr. Leitch on October 1.
May I ask the right hon. gentleman how he received it?

Well, I will tell him. Apparently a moment ago the Prime Minister did not know he had received it. I would point out that a copy of the telegram was sent to me. Apparently the Prime Minister paid so little attention to it he did not know from what I was reading.
There was a further telegram sent to the Minister of Labour by Mr. Leitch complaining that there had been no opportunity given to his company to make representations. The other day in the house I suggested that Mr. Wirtz or representatives of his department had warned that no other ships of this company should be allowed to go to Chicago. I will return to that a little later, because I find that a representative of one of the unions quoted the United States labour department as having stated that Mr. Wirtz had informed him that it would be dangerous, if not indeed improper, for a Canadian ship to use the great lakes and continue on its course to the port of Chicago.
This morning we endeavoured to secure some information, and we received the usual brush-oif. Because of the series of evasive replies that have been received, the hon. member for Ontario moved a motion and that motion was not placed before the house by Mr. Speaker. I am not arguing in any way about that, the determination having been made. I would point out, however, that this is a matter of deep concern. It was a matter of deep concern in the month of August when this house adjourned. There was lawlessness and tyranny being perpetrated on the great lakes. A report was made by Mr. Justice Norris, and the government decided to adjourn parliament. Parliament adjourned. The minister had stated that if there was any outbreak of lawlessness, parliament would be recalled. There was a dynamiting. There may
Interim. Supply
have been, in addition to that, other acts of lawlessness to a lesser degree, but a dynamiting took place. I am not going to argue at the moment that therefore parliament should have been called between September 10 and 30, although that is a long delay on the part of a government that was full of determination to protect Canadian interests and the rights of Canadians to the use of the great lakes.
The house convened on September 30. Naturally we expected legislation then. First there was the promise that if certain things were done, this legislation would be proceeded with. Then, finally, the answer of the Prime Minister today indicates that it is now part of the Pearson plan that this legislation will not be brought before parliament until the hope of a private settlement is entirely terminated. That is passing strange. The resolution is here. I am sure the house as a whole would be willing to proceed immediately with it. Why the delay? Why these movements, these pilgrimages back and forth between here and Washington that have become so characteristic in the last few weeks and months, and so devoid of success?
Hear, hear.

What of these pilgrimages? Why has no action been taken? Why this delay? Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Ontario this morning endeavoured to bring this matter before the house. Let me point out this. He was minister of labour for a period of five and one half years or more. He gave to this country a degree of amity in labour relations that we had never enjoyed prior thereto. The minister suggested there was no pressure on the government. We realize they have a lot of problems on their hands. We recognize their difficulties. We see their faces showing the disconsolateness that comes from responsibility. We see all that, Mr. Chairman. But surely there has been time to take some action.
I am going to refer particularly now to the longshoremen's strike. I am not going to argue the question as to its legality. The Prime Minister smiles, Mr. Chairman. He does not even know what a legal strike is, judging from his lack of knowledge of a few minutes ago of a wire he received pointing out the great seriousness of the situation that prevails. Here we are with tremendous orders for available wheat that is waiting to be shipped. Apparently 60 million bushels of wheat are ready for shipment at the port of Montreal or are en route there. What has the government done? Why did it wait until the last minute of the last hour before acting? There are 3,800 members of the

Interim Supply
international longshoremen's association in Montreal, Three Rivers, Quebec and Sorel. These ports handle an average of 75 ships a day at the peak of the shipping season. Montreal alone can load 3 million bushels of grain per day.
There were long negotiations with the shipping federation. This is not a recent matter. Last March the federation offered the I.L.A. a 12 cents an hour increase, plus 4 cents in fringe benefits. The I.L.A. refused. The executive accepted, but the membership declined. A conciliation board was set up. It unanimously recommended a 22 cents package. Both parties rejected the recommendation. Then came the wildcat strike on the waterfront on September 9 and 10. Then the government, with the Russian wheat deal on the books, saw the need for some action and proceeded to act. The cause of this strike was rank and file dissatisfaction with dragged out negotiations with the shipowners; the members of the union were fed up with the delay. The union leaders persuaded the members to return to work, and shortly after the conciliation board report was brought in.
Why was there such delay after the report? This is just another example of the government's complete lack of decisiveness. It makes plans, but they are mainly theory without action. This is just another example of that. The government apparently saw no urgency in the situation until the Russian wheat shipments were in jeopardy. This is one time they cannot rely on Mr. Wirtz or anyone else outside our country. The attitude to date in so far as the Montreal, Three Rivers, Quebec and Sorel situation is concerned has been that of too little and too late. On Wednesday the government appointed as federal mediator Judge Lippe of Montreal. Why all the delay? Why wait until the last moment?
Some hen. Members: Oh, oh.

The Prime Minister
laughs. That is the way he tries to laugh off the seriousness of Canadian problems that he is beginning to realize. He laughs; that is his attitude.

Mr. Chairman, in view of the fact that the right hon. gentleman has mentioned my name, I may tell him that I am laughing at his suggestion that there was delay in making an appointment which was made immediately after the time it could have been made; and I remind him of the year and a half delay in appointing the chairman of the board of the C.N.R.
What a comparison that is.

Mr. Chairman, the Prime Minister smiles when he is most annoyed and hurt. There is a guilty conscience there. Why did he mention the C.N.R. presidency? If you could have seen the face of the Minister of Justice today, Mr. Chairman, you would have understood that the Prime Minister has his troubles.
He can make decisions, though.
All I can say in this connection is that the House of Commons breathes more freely today. I do not know how he could have stood the loss of the Minister of Justice.
Or the Minister of National Defence.

I can understand why the Prime Minister referred to that matter. Nothing has been done. There has been nothing but delay. Smokescreens of that kind do not deter me from placing the facts before the house. Shipping is tied up. Newspaper reports claim that officials hope to divert wheat and flour loading to other ports. I will make reference to that a little later. The hon. member for Saint John-Albert has been endeavouring to secure some consideration for Saint John and Halifax, and the hon. member for Churchill has placed a very strong argument before the house on behalf of the port of Churchill, which for some reason was circumvented under these plans.
What is going to be done about this? We would like to know what is the situation. Why the delay? The government realized it would need the ships and shipping facilities when it entered into this contract. The Minister of Trade and Commerce pointed out that at our seaports approximately 640 vessels each of 10,000 tons average would be required to transport the wheat. This house needs from the government a statement, not the evasion of the last few days, setting forth what it is going to do; for the minister must be the first to admit it is imperative that there be no interference with the smooth flow of loading and shipping if there is any expectation of commitments being met.
The house cannot tolerate a situation of this kind, because the prospect of continuing violence and disruption on the seaway and the lakes threatens interference with free movement on these waters. I repeat that the information given to me, despite the fact that it has not come to the notice of the Minister of Labour, is that the S.I.U. threatened that if any action were expected or anticipated under the Norris report, there would be difficulty in Montreal.
Mr. Chairman, would the right hon. gentleman give us the source of that very important information?
I am making the statement, Mr. Chairman, and I do not have to give the source. I am saying that everybody knows it but the government.
Hear, hear.
If everybody knows it, why won't the right hon. gentleman tell us the source?

I might also add that the Minister of Labour was directly asked the question by a member of the press gallery on Saturday last, as to whether this took place, and my information is that his answer was "I am not going to discuss that."

Mr. Chairman, I think this point is of some consequence. It is true that last Saturday at the airport a member of the press gallery asked me had I any comment to make on a report that had been issued and put on the air during my absence from Ottawa, to the effect that there was this relationship between the I.L.A. and the S.I.U., and I said I had no comment. I went on to say that I hoped reason would prevail, a bit of advice which I would tender to the right hon. gentleman.

There is no denial that the answer was he had nothing to say about that. In so far as the minister's advice is concerned I say, physician heal thyself.
I shall go on from there. I have mentioned this threat which is common knowledge, and it is also suggested in the wires to which I have made reference. Why has there been the delay in action? It is a strange thing that all through the past Mr. Banks has received the kindest of treatment from successive Liberal governments.
I am going to refer to that because it is strange that here the government says to the House of Commons, "We have a resolution on the order paper and we are going to act on it." Then the government suddenly changes its tone today and says, "We will get on with it only if we do not get a private arrangement."
Many people are involved, including Mr. Meaney, Mr. Paul Hall and representatives of the United States department of labour. It is very obvious there is a difference of opinion, and that what is good for Canada is not regarded by Mr. Wirtz, and those associated with him, as good for the United States. That has been made very clear, and there are many quotations I could give of statements and conclusions to that effect by members of the press gallery following the interview they had with him.
Interim Supply
In behind all these things we have the shadow of Mr. Banks and the solicitude this man has received from successive Liberal governments, this man who Mr. Justice Norris said is of the stuff of the Capones and of the Hoffas. Throughout his career he has been protected by the Liberal party in this country. He was given, after conviction in Canada, the unassailable status of landed immigrant.
What manner of man is this demi-god? When he came to Canada and signed the immigration entry paper the question was not there and was not asked: "Have you a criminal record?" That would have been an embarrassing question because his criminal record would have kept him out.
In those days the minister was Hon. Walter Harris.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Would the right hon. gentleman permit a question?
Certainly.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Could the right hon. gentleman say on what date Mr. Banks first came to Canada?

I have got everything and I am very glad that question has been asked. I did not think I would have the opportunity to put it all on the record, and I thank my hon. friend because this is very helpful. I will give him the entire record, because he has asked for it.
I have previously mentioned Mr. Banks' criminal record and I will deal with the items one by one, including the hon. gentleman's question. Mr. Banks lived in the United States and had a criminal record from 1930 until 1947. He faced various charges upon which he was convicted, and I will come to the date in a moment.
After his arrival in Canada a series of charges were preferred against him from time to time and finally, on April 14, 1952, he was convicted at Montreal on a charge of being in possession of smuggled United States cigarettes, to which he pleaded guilty. After that he was immediately subject to deportation, but nothing was done about it. No action was taken to deport him on the basis of his conviction.
I have the order in council here, and it is interesting reading. I will not belabour the committee with it at this time, but I have it for future use.
Mr. Banks came to Canada in January, 1949. He entered as a non-immigrant with a minimum of formality, that minimum of formality consisting of failing to ask him the question that would have kept him out. From 1949 onward his period of stay was extended in six months periods, and on May 8, 1952, he applied for the status of landed immigrant.

Interim Supply
The hon. gentleman who has asked me the question about the date of his arrival did not become minister of citizenship and immigration until July 1, 1954.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman has that fact correct.

But it is of interest that this order in council was passed during his term of office. In June, 1954, Mr. Jean St. Onge of the Montreal office of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration, designated as an inquiry officer under section 11 of the immigration act, recommended Mr. Banks' deportation on the basis of his criminal record involving moral turpitude.
In June, 1954 Mr. Banks appealed to the then minister of citizenship and immigration, Mr. Harris, against deportation, and there was an amendment introduced in the House of Commons, and passed through parliament, enabling an appeal to be made to the minister against such orders. I am sure hon. gentlemen opposite would say that it was only coincidence-
Did you vote against that?

-but it had a wonderful effect. It enabled the appeal to be heard by Mr. Harris, and in the same month Mr. Harris allowed the appeal and set aside the deportation.
I am glad the Secretary of State asked me this question, because it clears up the atmosphere. I will now refer to the order in council, because it was passed during the period when he was minister. Mind you, I should point out that the determination was made earlier, after parliament ended. Parliament ended near the end of June and the appeal was then allowed, with the order in council being passed, and this order shows a masterful capacity for forgetting the facts. Attached to it is his record, and that order in council is P.C. 1954-1015, dated July 6, 1954, and reads as follows:
The committee of the privy council have had before them a report dated 30th June 1954, from the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, representing:
That under section 5 of the Immigration Act, a person who has been convicted of or admits having committed any crime involving moral turpitude is prohibited from admission to Canada;
That notwithstanding this prohibition the governor general in council mayand this was the effect of the amendment passed by the House of Commons-
-upon satisfactory evidence of successful rehabilitation, authorize the admission of such a person to Canada if a period of five years in the case of an adult and two years in the ease of a minor has elapsed since the termination of the imprisonment period or the completion of the sentence; and
That the person named in the appendix hereto appears to have been successfully rehabilitated.

The committee, therefore, on the recommendation of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration,-
That was not the hon. member for Bonavis-ta-Twillingate. He had not become minister at the time the recommendation was made. He was just the minister at the time the order in council was passed.
-advise that Your Excellency may be pleased, pursuant to the Immigration Act to authorize the admission to Canada of Harold Chamberlain Banks, of whom particulars are set out in the appendix hereto.
This appendix is really something. It is what you might call an abbreviated appendix. No operation has ever been more complete in removing from an appendix the serious portions of it. All it says is that Harold Chamberlain Banks was convicted on September 27, 1930 by the Los Angeles superior court and sentenced to 14 years in San Quentin. The document goes on:
Twenty years have elapsed since the termination of the sentence. He entered Canada at intervals from 1948 as representative of the seafarers' international union and has resided here since 1952. He has been executive director of the union...
In view of his important contribution to the Canadian shipping industry, it is recommended that authority for his admission be provided under section 5(d) (i) of the Immigration Act.
I said this was an abbreviated appendix. They forgot to mention that he was convicted of having smuggled goods in his possession only two years earlier, an offence for which he could be deported but which, for some reason or other, was not mentioned in the record. This is no attempt to deal completely with the record he has. That has already been dealt with in the Norris report. Look at the situation. Review that evidence, and ask yourselves whether Harold Chamberlain Banks has not got a great deal to thank the former Liberal government for. I wonder whether the solicitude shown in 1952, 1953 and 1954 by the governments of that day will be forgotten by the Canadian people.
That is the picture. Today this man enjoys the status of landed immigrant with established Canadian domicile although citizenship has been refused to him. He applied for citizenship but his application was refused. When we were in office we looked into this situation to see what could be done. We found that as a result of the action taken by the former government under the order in council to which I have alluded there was no action which we could take against him. That shows how complete, how thorough a job was done in assuring Mr. Banks that whatever his lawlessness might be he could not be interfered with as far as his residence and domicile in Canada are concerned.

I answered one, and I have not completed-

I ask, why the failure of the government to act? Why all this playing around? When I asked the minister the other day whether Mr. Wirtz had tried to stop a Canadian grain ship he said he had no information. All I can tell him is that it was in the press on September 27. I have the clipping here.
Washington (CP)-U.S. labor secretary Willard Wirtz will attempt to use his influence to discourage a Toronto company from sending another grain ship to Chicago, a trade union source said Thursday night.
The informant said Wirtz made this promise in a brief discussion Thursday with Peter McGavin, secretary treasurer of the AFL-CIO maritime trade department.
Earlier, McGavin told a press conference that any move to send the grain ship John Ericsson to Chicago would be considered a deliberate provocation designed to stir up new trouble in the great lakes labor battle.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Is that evidence?

Why, what manner of work is this?
May I call it one o'clock?

Mr. Chairman, I have not gone into lengthy detail in answer to my hon. friend, the Secretary of State. There are many more details that could be given and will be given at an appropriate time in regard to Banks' record. I have simply given a general outline and have left out quite a series of events in the Alger story of Mr. Banks' life. I can, of course, deal with these matters in more detail on another occasion. However, I feel I have answered the question asked.
I would point out that various questions were asked in the House of Commons in June of 1954 regarding Mr. Banks, and Hansard records the discussions that took place. I would refer particularly to Hansard of the 26th of June, 1954, page 6825, where reference was made by Mr. Harris, the then minister, to the Immigration Act with regard to an appeal to the minister of an order to
Interim Supply
deport and the exercise of clemency by him on grounds of satisfactory proof of rehabilitation.
The record of Mr. Banks in Canada, apart altogether from the conviction for having in his possession smuggled goods, was sufficient for his deportation.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I wonder whether the right hon. gentleman would permit me to ask him one question. Was there any other conviction in Canada? I am afraid I have not made a careful study of the record recently such as the right hon. gentleman has, but was there any other conviction in Canada except the one for being in possession of smuggled cigarettes?

I did not expect that would be asked. I have the record and I will endeavour to locate it. I may have it here and as I come to it I will deal with that point, because the question is a perfectly proper one. I know that the minister is very much interested in the position of Mr. Banks because it was during his period of office that the order in council was passed; but the direction was made by Mr. Harris a day or so before he turned over his portfolio to the hon. gentleman. You see, parliament stopped sitting on the 26th of June and in those four days-I know the minister will agree that the department works very fast-the department operated at an unusual speed. The minister looked into the whole question and, while he expressed doubts that a decision would be made at an early date, within four days a decision had been rendered.
The decision, of course, must have been a decision of cabinet. Indeed, there are records showing that generally speaking not only did the principle of cabinet solidarity apply but the Secretary of State gave his personal imprimatur to the high quality of Mr. Banks. There is one hon. gentleman in the house who used to take a very firm stand on this question. I refer to the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) who has turned in my direction now. He dealt with this matter at length on a number of occasions but did not receive much consideration.
During the noon hour Maclean's magazine for February, 1955, Canada's national magazine, was brought to my attention. It contains an article dealing with the appeal in question and says:
Banks appealed to the minister of the department, Walter Harris. In his last day of office, before taking over the finance ministry, Harris quashed the deportation order.
Then it goes on to say:
Harris' successor. Jack Pickersgill, says, "I wholeheartedly agree with Walter Harris' decision. I hope that a lot of questions will be asked about it.''
In addition, there were other ministers who decided to add their enthusiastic support to

Interim Supply
Mr. Banks. Among them was the labour minister of that time and, according to Maclean's magazine, again the Secretary of State supported Mr. Banks with his personal judgment.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: With what?
His personal judgment.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I must confess, Mr. Chairman, that I do not understand what that statement means. It does not seem to me to make much sense. But if I may say one word I think it is probably correct, though I have forgotten the article, that I did say I agreed with the decision that Mr. Harris had made.
I am perfectly sure that Mr. Harris made that decision as he made every other decision, in the full knowledge of his duty to this country-
Order.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: -and no man did so more conscientiously.

The hon. gentleman said he was rising to ask a question. He just makes the situation that much worse by again giving his support to the course that was followed that was so detrimental to Canada. He now embraces Banks once more.
Nonsense.
The degree to which he again embraces Banks indicates that Mr. Banks has friends in government circles.
Nonsense.
A question was asked of me, and that question referred to any other charges-

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, I said conviction. I asked the right hon. gentleman if Mr. Banks had been convicted in Canada before June 30 of any other charge except the one he mentioned. I said "convicted", not charged. Whatever the right hon. gentleman may feel about it, I do not feel that a charge is a conviction.
Hear, hear.
Another friend of Banks.

I now want to appropriate the words of the hon. gentleman during an interruption a moment ago. He said, "I am not in the habit of repudiating my friends". The whole story now becomes unveiled-my friend Banks; he is not in the habit of repudiating him.
They are both sailors.

The seriousness of the situation along the St. Lawrence is shown by the telegram I received a few moments ago from Mr. A. P. Gleave, president of the national farmers' union. He says:

I have sent the following telegram to Prime Minister Pearson. Strike of longshoremen union creates intolerable situation of bringing grain movement through St. Lawrence ports to a standstill thus jeopardizing completion of grain sales to Soviet union and other countries during the current crop year. Resumption of grain movement is of vital interest to western farmers and general economy. Therefore we urge immediate legislative action.
This is an example of how serious the situation is, and of the need for immediate action.
I have already pointed out the tremendous delays from August until now. I am not going to quote Hansard to cite the reasons for the delay in taking action. The undertaking given by the government was clear and unequivocal. It was this: If disorder were to break out, if tyranny were to again ride, parliament would be called back. Days have gone by since, and yet the government continues to fritter away time by meetings, considering, discussing. I said a moment ago that there seemed to be a relationship between the situation that has arisen in Montreal and the action threatened to be taken by the government in relation to Mr. Banks.
It is interesting to go back as far as November 22, 1960 to find a beautiful picture of brotherly love. The Secretary of State said: "I am not in the habit of repudiating friends." Here they are together, the five leaders, attending a union conference at S.I.U. headquarters. They are as follows:	Thomas
Gleason, general secretary of the international longshoremen's association; Hal C. Banks, vice president, seafarers' international union and director of its Canadian district; Paul Hall, who called the conference, president of the S.I.U. and the maritime trades department of the AFL-CIO; Tony Anastasia, vice president of the I.L.A., and Rod Hayes, vice president of the international brotherhood of teamsters.
Now, Mr. Chairman, there is the aggregation. They are all together there in one picture. The article says they are agreed all legal means of action will be taken to stop the operation of British vessels in competition with Canadian ships. Anastasia is gone, and his son-in-law now runs things. Paul Hall is the man who is telling Canadians what they can do. He wants Canada to fall into line with his ideas. What manner of system is this, whereby Canadians are being told by Paul Hall what they should do? To the credit of Mr. Jodoin, I must say he made it quite clear that he, for one, was not going to take that kind of dictation. I want to emphasize that fact.
Now, we are looking forward to hearing from the government in connection with this matter. I have just touched the fringes. This was in answer to a question, as you know,

Mr. Chairman. I dislike taking so much time to answer a question, but I had to do it.
Now then, can we tolerate the situation, the prospect of continuing violence and disruption on the seaway? Can we tolerate the autocratic interference with the free movement of shipping? Is that not intolerable at any time? Can we allow the perpetuation of tyranny perpetrated by this man Banks who enjoys the position of being the pampered pet of the former Liberal government? Today the Secretary of State said, in effect, I will not desert my friends. This situation must be faced, but I am not going to disagree with the minister that if he can arrive at a system whereby Banks will be out, directly or indirectly, with no control over Canada, it will be welcomed on every hand. In any event, if any settlement which so many across the line are trying to bring about removes Banks from Canada physically but still allows him, directly or indirectly, control over Canada, it will not be tolerated by this parliament and cannot be accepted by the Canadian people.
I will say no more at this time. There is a great deal more in the record. I found that revealing it part by part is always more effective than producing the entire record at once. I now leave it to the government to say why all the delay, why the playing around, why the procrastination? We have had six months of this government. The record has been one of continued postponement, failure to act, much planning, uncertainty and incoherence. There has been a complete denial of unity as between ministers occupying portfolios in the same government. I ask the government, what are you going to do about this? Are you going to instal Hal Banks as the uncrowned king over the rights of Canadians?

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a very brief statement in respect of the two major issues that have been raised by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition. One has to do with the serious development that began this morning at Montreal and which extends to the ports of Quebec and Three Rivers. This morning I suggested that we ought to keep this situation in perspective. The strike that began this morning had been in effect for only three and a half hours when the hon. member for Ontario proposed that the house be adjourned in order that the opposition may belabour the government for failing to take what he described as effective action to deal with this situation.
I stated that this strike is fully lawful; it is legal under Canadian law. The right hon. gentleman thought my statement this morning would be regarded as a classic one. Well, I doubt whether it will ever have that high
Interim Supply
station. But it certainly underlines my belief in free labour, not slave labour.
Hear, hear.

It underlines my belief in free collective bargaining. It underlines my belief in the right to strike as a part of that process of free collective bargaining which is fully protected under Canadian labour law and which is one of the fundamental rights of Canadian workers. I am surprised that any hon. gentleman would suggest that at this stage the government ought to have moved to remove this fundamental right from this class of Canadian workers.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Nobody said that.

There can be no other interpretation placed on the intervention of the hon. member for Ontario and the Leader of the Opposition. The alternative to moving rapidly to prevent this right to strike was to follow the course that was followed by the Canadian government, and that was to appoint a mediator in order to bring the parties together.
Too late.

I believe this decision was the correct decision in the circumstances. I ought to remind hon. gentlemen opposite that this dispute is not of recent origin. The dispute or the lack of agreement between the shipping federation and the longshoremen is not a development of recent days or even recent months. It began with the termination of the contracts on December 31, 1962. There were two offers made with regard to which the shipping federation agreed and the officers of the locals agreed. These offers were submitted to the membership, and my understanding is that on both occasions these offers were turned down by the membership. The first, as I understand it, occurred in January of this year, and the second in February and March, when the full powers for amity ascribed to the hon. member for Ontario by the Leader of the Opposition could have been fully employed. But the fact is that notwithstanding the best efforts of the hon. member for Ontario, this dispute was not resolved though two sincere efforts-and I believe they were sincere efforts-were made under his direction to resolve them; or at least, there was one effort made under the aegis of the Department of Labour.
The next development was the appointment of a conciliation board, which is provided for under Canadian law. The chairman, Judge Lafleur, was nominated by both parties and he rendered his decision. He secured a unanimous conclusion as a result of his deliberations. The conciliation board report

Interim Supply
was made public on Monday of this week. It had been released to the parties earlier and it was submitted to the membership of the union last Sunday. On Sunday last the membership decided not to accept the unanimous recommendation. Then, in the light of that development, it was up to the government of Canada to decide at what stage a mediator could be most effectively employed. This is a judgment that has to be made in the circumstances, and depends on the judgment of experienced officers of the labour department who have assessed the situation. It would have been easy to rush in on Monday and appoint a mediator, or on Tuesday. Our judgment was that the time to appoint a mediator was on Wednesday. We proceeded to appoint him on that day and he has been working ever since. I suggest that any earlier appointment would have been indiscreet and unwise in the circumstances.
The fact is that the mediator is at work with the parties. He is still in active contact with both groups as of this moment. Surely it is right on the part of the government to say that the mediator ought to be given full opportunity to explore the situation before the government takes further action or considers further action. I noticed, Mr. Chairman, that the right hon. gentleman did not make any proposal as to what ought to be done.
He hasn't any.
There was no proposal put forward because in the circumstances the government is taking the only possible and sensible course.
Hear, hear.

We realize this is a serious situation. Of course we do. And we are as concerned about it as any hon. member in the house or any other person. But we intend to take whatever action is necessary in the light of developments in the mediation process.
That is the situation. There has been no delay. The normal lawful procedures have been followed by the Canadian government that ought to have been followed. I suggest it was premature to raise the matter as a matter of debate today. If the desire had been to reach a settlement, then all of us ought to have applied to ourselves a self-denying ordinance until the work of the mediator could have proceeded further.
The farmers of western Canada will not agree with you.
