Mr. Chairman, may I say a word about that aspect of the problem, with respect to the imposition of a public trusteeship. The government of Canada received a report of an industrial inquiry commission that had been set up by the former government, an act that had been undertaken by the government only after the St. Lawrence seaway closed. Despite repeated requests by the Canadian labour movement to the government to take some action to deal with this problem, the government refused to take any action until it was forced to do so following the closing of the St. Lawrence seaway by the Canadian labour movement. That was the way in which the government of the day acted. Those are the circumstances in which the commission was appointed.
We received the report of the commission and within a matter of two weeks the government decided to accept the major recommendation of the Norris inquiry, namely to impose a public trusteeship on all the maritime transportation unions. Before making that decision we had consulted with the Canadian Labour Congress. We had secured its co-operation. We had received the full assurance of all affected unions, save and except the S.I.U., that they would accept the trusteeship in the interests of cleaning up what all of us admit is a dreadful situation in this particular segment of the Canadian labour movement on the great lakes. There is no difference between us on that point.
I hesitate to review again the circumstances which obliged the government to delay the introduction of legislation until this particular part of the session. But the fact of the matter is that the officials of the justice department advised the government that it would be impossible to prepare the legislation, to examine each of the constitutions, each of the collective agreements in a short time; that this work would take most of the summer. And that work did take most of the summer. We have a resolution on the order paper. We had a bill ready and it will be introduced if and when this resolution is accepted by the House of Commons. Surely that is sufficient evidence of the determination of this government to proceed along the lines of its announced policy of last July.
When this decision was made it was evident in this house that any person who believed in free labour felt that the house of labour should be given an opportunity to put its own house in order before the government would step in with what each of us regarded as an unprecedented act. That is why the pilgrimages have been undertaken; that is why the travels have been made. It has been in an effort to provide an opportunity for an interunion arrangement that

would be entered into by the Canadian labour centre in Ottawa and the United States labour centre in Washington. If at any time the Canadian labour movement says that the terms that may be under discussion are unacceptable, that ends the matter. It is a decision that must first be made by the Canadian Labour Congress in the light of its responsibilities to its own members. That is why in this past week I have not asked the house to deal with this resolution, because I thought this effort had to be continued until we were all assured that it offered no possibilities.
I want to assure you, Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, that just as soon as I am convinced, and the government is convinced, an effective alternative is not possible with a private arrangement, the Canadian government will proceed at once with its public trusteeship legislation.

Would the minister permit a question? If I understood him correctly he stated in regard to the longshoremen's dispute that the only possible line of action for the federal government was the appointment of a mediator.

Mr. Chairman, it seems to me there are two major alternatives, either to stop the normal course of collective bargaining by preventing a strike by law at this stage, or to pursue that other line of reaching a settlement through the mediation process, and surely mediation would be the first step to secure a settlement without the imposition of Canadian law?

I asked the minister that question because the other day, in answer to a question put by the hon. member for Ontario, he stated that mediation was only one of several possible steps that could be taken by the government. I wonder if he would now reveal what these other steps might be.
I think in the circumstances it would be quite imprudent, as I have already stated, to prejudice the work of the mediator by indicating what further lines might be followed.

Mr. Chairman, I am glad that the Leader of the Opposition has used this opportunity to bring before us a matter of grave and urgent importance, and that is the breakdown of law and order as revealed by the Norris report.
I know that my hon. friend, the Minister of Labour, is struggling with a difficult situation. I know he has to listen to advice and put up with the pressure of many people and many interests, and I for one do not blame him for seeking consultation with his opposite number in the government of the
Interim Supply
United States; because that government is, and may well be, directly concerned with the matters in question here. Indeed, it is the duty of the minister to keep in touch with his opposite number in the United States government. I share, along with the other members of this party-and I think I dare speak for all hon. members of the committee, or most of the hon. members-and most of the Canadian people, a very deep distaste for any suggestion of government intervention by trusteeship in the internal affairs of a trade union, or indeed of any other voluntary organization.
But, Mr. Chairman, I want to repeat, reiterate and re-echo one thing that the Leader of the Opposition said, and that is that I do not believe the people of Canada will tolerate any sort of a compromise, or so-called solution, that in any manner, direct or indirect, leaves Banks or his associates in a position in which they can influence in any way the future of the maritime unions of Canada.
Mr. Banks has been described in loving detail, not only by Mr. Justice Norris but, in his own inimitable style, by the Leader of the Opposition. I will not attempt to rival their colourful language, but may I be permitted to summarize in my own way Banks' achievements in this country.
He was able to use a trade union, with the co-operation of shipping companies, to undermine and destroy democracy in an important section of the trade union movement. He was able to establish a reign of terror on the Canadian waterfront. He was able to employ fraud and defamation to achieve his purposes and enrich himself at the expense of Canadian seamen. Above all, he was able to defy the laws of the country openly and repeatedly.
Throughout the long story of violence, intimidation and illegality, the law stood mocked and impotent. The fault was not the fault of the members of the S.I.U. They were cowed and intimidated. Those who attempted to employ the democratic rights conferred on them by the union constitution were victims of violence or were soon without a job. The fault did not lie in the organized trade union movement of this country. Four years ago the S.I.U. was expelled from the ranks of legitimate trade unions in Canada.
The fault lies with Banks himself and his associates, and it also lies with the shipping companies who conspired with Banks to mock and to defeat the law of this country. Furthermore, it lies with the complete failure of law enforcement by those responsible for it. It lies with laws that lack teeth, and it lies with the effective exercise of influence in high places.

Interim Supply
Today the Leader of the Opposition, as is his wont, sought to make great political capital out of the failures of the previous Liberal administration. I must agree with some of his structures; but since he is fond of biblical quotations I will give him one or two to ponder. "Let him who is without fault"-I should say sin-"cast the first stone"; and there is another one about hypocrites casting the beams out of their own eyes. I apologize to the committee for stumbling over biblical quotations but I have not, like many other hon. members, been directly trained in theology.
I ask the Leader of the Opposition-and he does not need to answer me now-what happened in the battle against S.I.U. lawlessness during the years from 1957 to 1963 when the right hon. gentleman headed the government of this country? There are some revealing incidents reported in the Norris commission report. I do not propose to read from them at length, but at page 54 of that report there will be found a brief statement of what the personnel manager of the C.S.L. stated to the head of the union whose rights it was about to tear up at the request of Mr. Banks. He said:
Did you read the statement I made a couple of days ago before our management assocations? There are no teeth in the labour laws. Have a look at the act. First of all you have to go to the minister and get permission to prosecute. That will take you a couple of months. We will kick it around in the courts here for a year and if necessary we will take it to the Supreme Court of Canada. That will take about two years.
Then he says:
We have assurance from Mr. Banks of indemnification. By this time you will be out of business if you do not get your dues coming in, you know that. That is the way of life.
That is the head of the personnel department of the Canadian Steamship Lines speaking to the man whose rights he was about to tear up. The thing gets worse and worse, and this is what I want to test the Leader of the Opposition with, and see if he or his former minister of labour have any explanation.
A Mr. Scott Misener, the president of one of the smaller companies, writes a letter to Mr. Bernard Wilson, who appears to be a high official in the Canadian Department of Labour-the director of industrial relations. In that letter, which is dated 1959, he says this:
Dear Mr. Wilson:
This is to inform you that Scott Misener Steamships Limited and Misener Holdings Limited have signed an agreement with the seafarers' international union of North America-licensed division.
This, of course, we realize is against the Labour Relations Act but, under the circumstances that I have explained to you, we have no alternative but to do so. There is also a copy enclosed of a

letter from Mr. Banks indemnifying our companies from any lawsuits, etc. that may arise out of signing of his agreement.
So, Mr. Chairman, I call the attention of members of the committee to the fact that as early as 1959, when the administration headed by the right hon. gentleman was in power, a high official of the Department of Labour was informed by the president of a steamship company that he proposed to defy the law, to tear up his agreement with another union, and to enter into an agreement with Banks that he knew was illegal.
He informed the Department of Labour of this fact in 1959 and he forwarded a copy of the indemnification agreement in which Banks had the insolence to write and say to the effect, "If you disregard the law of Canada I will indemnify you against the result."
Absolutely nothing happened.
We appointed the Norris commission.

Yes, in 1962, three years later; and the reason for that was because a union, the Canadian brotherhood of transport workers, tied up the Welland canal as a demonstration that the government had to take action; and it was forced to take action in 1962, three years later.
I think the important question which faces the people of Canada is this: how long should we tolerate this sort of lawlessness? I repeat: it will not do to have any solution or so-called solution which involves agreement with those who have broken the laws. I know the Minister of Justice is receiving a report from his legal advisers as to possible prosecutions arising out of the matters with which we are dealing. All I can say is that those responsible for this defiance of the law, whether they be Banks and his associates or whether they be steamship companies, should be prosecuted for their defiance and evasion of the laws of this country.
May I ask the hon. member a question? May I ask him whether he has acted as solicitor for the S.I.U. at any time?

I could give the hon. gentleman a technical answer; the answer is, no. But I have acted as counsel for Mr. Banks for a short period in a libel action. I should have thought the hon. member for Ontario was sufficiently aware of the legal practices of this country to know that those who are engaged in their duty as counsel are in no way involved in the affairs of those for whom they happen to act, sometimes very briefly, as I did, in a purely technical matter some time ago. I have not been involved with Mr. Banks in any shape or form; neither has this party.

Now I want to ask the former minister of labour a question. Was he aware of this letter which was sent to his senior officials, and why was no action taken? Let the hon. gentleman answer that question. A little less of this "holier than thou" attitude on the part of the official opposition would be helpful in reaching a solution of the issues raised by these serious matters.
I do not think there is anything further I can add except to say that we in this house, without casting stones at each other, should consider very seriously the grave issues which have been raised, and even though it may be necessary to do unprecedented or distasteful things we should make sure we take action which goes to the root of the grave situation disclosed by the Norris report.

Mr. Chairman, since we have been criticizing a labour leader for the past two hours, I trust that my colleagues will allow me to make a critical review of the past record of the two old parties.
Not so very long ago, and we still remember it today, when the government party sat on this side of the house with us, we often heard them criticize the indecision of the then Conservative administration, the government of indecision, they called it, for the past five years. 1 wonder today, after a few months of administration by the present government, whether the people are not telling themselves: we no longer have a government of indecision but a government of bad decisions.
Mr. Chairman, when one considers the change of attitude and the about-turn effected within barely a year in our country by the members of the two old parties, one wonders if that would not actually be the basis on which the people could pass judgment on them, perhaps more easily than we think.
When we consider especially their about-face, following the remarks made last night by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas), I think that our Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) would deserve, in the opinion of the Canadian people, the title of minister of war.
Hardly a year ago, we heard statements for and against nuclear weapons; we accepted them and signed a treaty through the Minister of National Defence. Contrary to the usual practice of the house, the treaty was not approved by the house, but the government made no bones about it and placed us before an accomplished fact.
We were blamed in the past for our indecision, for the failure to produce those very important documents concerning nuclear agreements with our neighbours. The same request is turned down today, and I wonder
Interim Supply
whether the title of minister of war would not be more appropriate than the one of Minister of National Defence.
As for the Department of Agriculture, we were informed recently that from now on the Canadian wheat board and wheat sales to foreign countries would come under the Department of Trade and Commerce. I remember that, last year, the then minister of agriculture had succeeded in disposing of a very large quantity of surplus Canadian wheat and the possibility, and there was even some discussion on the necessity of creating a second Department of Agriculture to meet the needs of this country. Today, we see a Department of Agriculture taking out the wheat board from that field in order to transfer it to the Department of Trade and Commerce. Of course I realize that it looks somewhat more commercial, a little more like trade; this happens perhaps because we are used to following in the steps of others and because we are closely linked with the most commercial country in the world which Great Britain was at one time, and because it is hoped that Canada will one day rank second among trading nations.
As far as the Minister of National Health and Welfare is concerned (Miss LaMarsh), I think that her case will be dealt with as quickly. The would-be mother of contributory pensions in Canada links the first legislation on pensions to a tax increase, to justify a raise of $10 a month for the beneficiaries of state pensions, those people who have given quite a few years of their lives to build this Canada which we, of this generation, inherit today. I, therefore, believe that it would hardly be wise to look upon her as the mother of pensions, more particularly if we think of the contributory pension scheme mentioned by her. When we look at the result, I wonder whether it is really of interest to sponsor such legislation. It has only led to further misunderstandings and another quarrel between two provinces and the federal state.
In regard to the President of the Privy Council who was made responsible for the survey on biculturalism, I wonder, like all those who are used to reading thrillers, if he is quite certain to be looked upon as agent X-13 in those suspense stories in regard to the promotion of bilingualism, when, in a recently established department, I mean the Department of Industry, we find that among the high officials who are occupying 230 key posts, all they had to say, in respect of the absence of bilingualism among the high officials of that department was: We could not go and take away officials having the required qualifications for those important functions from existing departments. Consequently, there are only unilingual people in charge of

Interim. Supply
the department. I would like to know whether the new agent X-13 is not being taken for a ride, as we would say among French Canadians.
Now let us consider other decisions. We have also a Post Office Department. I still remember and it was not so long ago, hardly six months, the various inquiries made by today's Postmaster General (Mr. Denis) who wanted to know whether the then postmaster general, (Mrs. Fairclough) had not thought of putting some mint-flavoured glue on the back of stamps because, as he said, it had been tried in some countries.
The hiring of additional mailmen was also sought on various occasions or during the Christmas period. In addition, an increase of expenditures by the Post Office Department was asked. I am wondering today if, instead of speaking of mint-flavoured glue on the back of stamps, the Canadian people are not tasting a famous fish glue with the increase of postal rates in the country?
And that is not all. According to a statement made in the house by the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette), I wonder if we should not do as previously proposed in certain provinces, that is establish a department of patronage in the Liberal party.
Let us consider another department, the Department of Finance. I still remember that, during the last election campaign, our hon. friends opposite went around in Quebec making fun of the utopian formula of Social Crediters; I wonder what solutions the economists of the Liberal party have found and especially the Minister of Finance who seeks advice, everyone knows where, to draw up his new budget.
I wonder what the people think of this new 11 per cent tax on materials, which has been withdrawn to be replaced by a 4 per cent tax? I wonder if this action was not taken to enable powerful trusts to purchase and store surplus materials which they will later put up for sale to realize supplementary profits when small contractors do not even have the necessary means nor the credit to promote their own little businesses. In my opinion, those are bad policies and decisions.
The same applies to a chairman of the Canadian stock exchange or a chairman of the Montreal stock exchange.
The 30 per cent tax on foreign investments is withdrawn and the tax on materials against small businessmen is maintained. Taxes against the powerful interests are withdrawn.
Mr. Chairman, I think that the people realize today that the mighty are in a position to defend themselves and that those who should be protected are always exploited and subjected to the increase in the cost of living

on account of a system which has been supported here thanks to the two old parties.
And what about the president of the stock exchange, who today is the Quebec minister of revenue and who, through a feat of strength, succeeded in convincing the Minister of Finance to remove his 30 per cent tax on foreign investments in Canada? I wonder if such an action was not especially designed to neutralize the evolution now taking place in Quebec.
In my opinion, that is something the people once again will be called upon to judge. As a matter of fact, the people may be called upon to pass judgment on the old parties' attitude toward them sooner than we think.
A word now about the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Deschatelets) who, early this week, invited us to visit the world fair site during the week end.
Yet, it was only about 15 days ago, following the use of electronic brains and I.B.M. machines, that we were told that the world fair probably could not take place before 1969.
I quite understand the reason for electronic brains and I.B.M. machines when I consider that, in a country as big as ours, and especially in as large a province as that of Quebec, islands have to be built. I wonder whether there was not a special reason for electronic brains to be called upon to decide when the world fair will take place?
Maybe they wanted a way out in case the world fair should not be held in 1967, for fear of something happening like the demonstration which took place recently at the Place des Arts, in Montreal. If such demonstrations keep up, I feel it is because there is a reason for them.
Which one?

Mr. Chairman, my hon. friends may keep on interrupting me, their cutting in on me does not disturb me in the least. I am simply reminded of an old saying of the renowned fabulist: "Let men of good will do as they should do, and let others boohoo".
Mr. Chairman, I am fully aware of the heavy load of work which is weighing down our ministers, and more particularly the Secretary of State (Mr. Picker sgill). He attends regularly the meetings of this house, he has a lot of work to do, but in spite of all that his position is rather sticky. Indeed, when one has promised two flags to the Canadian people, it is extremely difficult to choose only one; when one has spoken of giving Canada two national anthems, it is not easy to decide upon a single one.

I realize that the Secretary of State is also tied up with the various problems of the C.B.C., and it pains me greatly to have to chide him, when I think of his tremendous task.
As for the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, two bills have been brought in during the present session: Bills C-83 and C-84, both relating to the Northwest Territories.
The purpose of these pieces of legislation seems to be the formation or the creation of two new Canadian provinces. Let us remember, however, that for 97 years our ten provinces, supposedly united by a con-federative pact, have witnessed constant bickering between federal and provincial authorities; I wonder whether it would be advisable today to create two new provinces? Unless, of course, the idea is for them to replace such provinces which are threatening to withdraw?
But the biggest bills introduced in the house during this session are those dealing with the north.
Mr. Chairman, we can also ask ourselves what all the members who hope some day to join the cabinet think, particularly following the election campaign launched in this country on February 7 last.
I wonder what the members are thinking who hope to become ministers or even the hon. member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis) and especially our ultra-nationalist member for the Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Sauve) who had so carefully prepared his speech on bilingualism in Canada. What was his reaction when he learned today of the reappointment of the chairman of the Canadian National Railways, even prior to his appearance before the sessional committee on railway, air lines' and navigation?
What do these hopeful members for a cabinet post think today of their party? During the election campaign the Liberals, and especially the member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville, talked about the rainfall of dollars that Social Crediters would cause to fall on the Quebec people. However, the people of Quebec did not see any dollar rainfall, but the country inherited a tax storm under the Liberal administration.
I understand that a program known as the 60 days of decision had been prepared. During that period, the economy was supposed to start rolling again, and the Canadian taxpayers' problems were to be settled by the Liberal team during that same period.
I wonder today whether the people are not thinking the matter over and wondering if
Interim Supply
the famous 60 days of decision are not in the process of becoming the tales of the Arabian nights.
I wonder if, after those Arabian nights, we will not have the story of Ali Baba and the 40 thieves.
Mr. Chairman, I understand also that, in some quarters, when a vote was taken recently, we were threatened and asked: Do you want an election? I can assure the house that it is not an election, near at hand or far off, that will impress those who represent the voice of the people here, those who had no election fund to wage their campaign. And, at that time, I could hear the voice of the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) who seemed greatly interested in finding out whether or not we wanted an election soon. I advise him not to worry because, at the next election, I will help him in Lotbiniere the same way he came to my help in my riding of Beauce.
You should come because your candidate lost his deposit.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The member who is speaking should not be interrupted, unless he agrees.

Mr. Chairman, I say it again, we are here not to represent the private interests of a group nor those of the financial powers of the country, but rather as representatives of the people who elected us to make heard the voice of those who are suffering and who, unfortunately, are forced to remain silent under the threat of patronage, afraid of the masters of finance and patronage.
We also want to make heard the voice of the people with regard to agriculture. There is on the order paper a resolution to appoint a minister of agriculture for eastern Canada, but we are still waiting for that measure to be presented. However, as head of that department, some bills have already been signed by the minister of agriculture for eastern Canada, and without anything having been done about his appointment.
What is being done about agriculture in the east? The premium on milk was abolished only a short time after the appointment mentioned. A sales tax on building materials, which affects farmers just as much as city workers, was levied.
Mr. Chairman, I wonder if those who speak of stimulating the economy to enable eastern farmers to take their rightful place in Canada are truly serious.
If the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hays) wants to fulfil every function and carry out every task, it seems to me that he should also be concerned with the lot of eastern

Interim Supply
farmers. He should look after families which have lived 25, 35, 50 or 100 years on the same farm, families of eight to ten people who have lived on the income from their farm and who, in 1963, when we have devised means of sending men to the moon, are unable to make a decent living with the income they derive from the family farm.
I can understand that schemes such as ARDA should be established, but do you know how the implementation of that program is envisaged by some people?
In some areas of the province of Quebec, a policy of what could be called decolonization is being practised.
We have an example of that in my own riding and in the constituency next to mine, Dorchester. This is what is being done under a plan of social welfare. Heads of families cannot make an honest living; they are unemployed six months a year because they go to work in the state of Maine. When they come back and find that they cannot live decently from the income of their farm, they submit a request for social assistance.
And what is done? The first advice they get is to leave their farm and to go and live in a village or a town. For, if they remain on their farm, they will not be able to benefit from social welfare legislation. But as soon as this family head leaves his farm, the Liberal party favorites of the community can be seen buying the farm to control it and then probably put it to use under ARDA. Or perhaps they want to establish collective farms? I do not know.
Mr. Chairman, would the hon. member allow me to ask him a question?

After I am through with my remarks.
Mr. Chairman, when we speak about the income of our farmers in eastern Canada, we do not speak through our hat if we say that their complaints are justified today. As a matter of fact, if we look at the figures tabled in the house on June 13, 1963, showing the average income of Canadian farmers, we can see that in 1950 their total income amounted to $1,219,757,000, while it reached $1,630,310,000, in 1962.
Using the same chart, it is noted that in 1950, the Quebec farmers' income was $211,416,000, whereas in 1962 it was only $179,668,000. Whereas there has been an increase in the farmers' revenue for the country as a whole, in the province of Quebec it has decreased from $211,416,000 to $179,668,000.
What is the reason for that situation, if not poor administration, and lack of foresight with respect to the needs of the eastern

farmers? This amply justifies the establishment of this new department of agriculture for eastern Canada, which will be in a better position to understand the needs of our farmers who are operating family farms.
Now, in order to give additional assistance to families, there is among social measures one called family allowances. We hear no more about it in Liberal circles.
I see that the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette) is applauding. I know he spoke about it in his constituency and I know that throughout the province of Quebec the Liberal party promised an increase in the family allowances immediately after the opening of the session.
It is untrue.
I still have in my desk a folder issued by my opponents. Not only did they mention it in their speeches, but in their written material as well.
It is false.

Is there a measure which requires more attention and more consideration? We have only to consider the hardship which prevails among large families.
I have here before me resolution No. 67 of the labour congress, which met in Philadelphia in 1947, wherein are clearly set forth the fundamentals underlying family allowances. I quote:
Society should normally co-operate with parents through general assistance measures designed to ensure the well-being of dependant children.
(1)	Public subsidies, in kind or in cash, or in both forms, should be used to bring up children in healthy surroundings, to help support children of large families and to supplement provisions for children who come under the family allowance plan.
(2)	When the aim is to bring up children in healthy surroundings, subsidies should be in the form of advantages such as free or cheap food for young children, school canteens and for families living in low rental housing units or having several children.
(3)	When the purpose is to help support large families or supplement provisions for children, by providing advantages in kind or provisions established under social insurance, subsidies should take the form of family allowances.
(4)	Such allowances should be paid, regardless of parents' income, according to a set scale that would represent a substantial contribution to the maintenance costs of the child and would make allowance for additional expenses required for older children.
That is a principle we should endeavour to follow more and more, because our economy must be increasingly distributive; otherwise we shall fall into collectivism, when individuals lose their personality and the family, the very foundation of society is dismembered. Collectivism will be detrimental to the family, and if we do not act promptly, we might have cause for regret.

So, Mr. Chairman, I suggest it is high time that we should raise the level of family allowances paid out under the family allowances act-and that as soon as possible-and at the same time set up a bonus system on milk production in order to help milk producers and provide for the setting up of secondary industries in our country.
At the present time, momentous changes are taking place in the province of Quebec, and we see more and more slogans like this one: "Masters in our own house". Such a slogan should not be only an election incentive. We can definitely become masters in our own house and for that purpose, we should first of all start thinking. I am aware of the sovereignty of the house over its own institutions, over the Bank of Canada and if there is one area where we should really use the Bank of Canada to handle new credits and thus increase the purchasing power, this is it. It is not for nothing that those social security acts catch the eye.
Instead of levying a 1 per cent personal income tax to pay for old age pensions, instead of postponing any longer the increase of family allowances, why do we not, on this one occasion, use the Bank of Canada, the same way it was put to work during the war when the time came to launch defence activities for the construction of war plants?
Then surely, it is high time, that we should use that same Bank of Canada; it is time that we should amend the Bank of Canada Act and that the bank should really work in the interest of the house, of the people and of the nation.
The Bank of Canada will be in the service of Canada when, without jeopardizing a sound economy, it will meet the needs of the human person. So long as we cannot satisfy the needs of the people, so long as we accept budgets, we will always be hamstrung by those budgets and we will never succeed in promoting the full flowering of every citizen by following a system which makes the human person subservient to money instead of money being in the service of man.
I wonder whether today we should not view that false philosophy in another light. Instead of moulding men, I wonder whether the government should not respect the yearnings of men and of families, allowing them to live as they should in a country with tremendous resources and a production which can meet the needs of one and all. Everybody needs food, clothing and adequate housing in the country. It is nothing else that is wished for by the Canadian people, by the farmers, the workers on the farm, in the city and in the plants.
28902-5-206
Interim Supply
The small businessman realizes very well that something is not running true within our present system. Most of the time, he is overburdened by taxes.
But come the next election campaign, our politicians will come back before the people and I think that once again, the province of Quebec will live up to its motto: "Je me souviens", which is close to our hearts.
May I ask a question?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Beauce's time having expired, he cannot be asked a question.

Mr. Chairman, this morning an effort was made to adjourn the house to discuss a matter of urgent public business. One of the reasons advanced in seeking this adjournment was the suggestion that, as a result of the type of motion now being discussed, we might not be able to concentrate our attention on this very urgent matter. Events of the last few minutes, I think, have indicated that this fear was valid. As we listened to the Minister of Labour making his serious-minded defence of the government today, I am sure it must have passed through the minds of many that here was a man dedicated to his own righteousness putting forward a group of platitudes, the like of which we have not heard in this house for many months.
Who is attacking the rights of free labour? Who is attacking the essential principles of freedom in this motion? There is no intention in our motion except the moving of this grain to the markets. Yet we have this red herring drawn across our path. And worse than that, the minister, by the type of statement he made, blamed for his own ineptness and the ineptness of his colleagues the civil servants in his own department. This was the significance of reading out all the steps he was taking. He was not content with putting the blame on the heads of his own department, but he also put it on the heads of the Department of Justice.
I think it is about time that the men who prowled this country in the years 1958, 1959, 1960 and 1961 saying they were confident that only they could govern Canada, and only they had the ability and experience to govern, should face up to the fact that they have made a miserable mess of their efforts in the last six months.
Amen.

When I hear a member of a Liberal government speaking about applying force to labour, I ask, who was the government in power in 1950 when the railway unions were forced to their knees by

Interim Supply
legislation passed in this very house by the party which now occupies the benches on the treasury side of the chamber? Our motion this morning was to provide an opportunity to explore the seriousness of the situation that is now before us. It was to give the house an opportunity to hear a statement from the government about what it planned to do to take advantage of this wonderful opportunity that had been given to us. I wonder if we fully understand the significance of this grain movement at this time in our economic history. It is not just a matter of moving 230 million bushels to the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. It is a matter of an opportunity to make sales of wheat to regular customers which, with the big sales to China and the extraordinarily large sale to Russia, would enable us to move this year close to 550 million bushels of wheat into foreign markets. This amount of wheat has a value of over $1 billion. This is the value of this one item of export alone. This means thousands of jobs for Canadian workers. This strike means, as the newspaper reports indicate, a loss of $2 million a day to the harbour of Montreal alone. On the sale of wheat to China alone it has been estimated that the port of Vancouver benefited to the extent of $48 million in wages to the men who worked on the dock, the longshoremen, in wages to the men who worked in the terminals, the railway workers, and so on. This sale surpasses by far even that tremendous over-all movement.
I would like to mention at this stage that the tremendous opportunity we have at the moment is being hurt, and perhaps nullified by the reluctance of this government to plan together, each member of the cabinet, and decide upon a course of action. This negligence on the part of the government is hitting the port of Montreal. That port, due to the economics of moving grain today, is becoming a marginal port. The whole economic tendency is to move grain further downstream and keep it below the ice in order that it may have access the year round to the markets of the world. This is the worst period for Montreal in which to have a strike. I point that out, Mr. Chairman, because this question involves not only the western farmer losing the sale of his grain, but we have a good, hard commercial competitor to the south who has over a billion bushels of grain to sell and who is willing to sell it, if I understand the newspaper reports correctly. Therefore I should like to suggest that this is not an ordinary labour dispute with management in which one should use the tried and true techniques of labour officials dealing with the matter of a strike in the ordinary 
way. This is a type of strike that hits at the vitals of the Canadian economy.
The Minister of Finance sits in his seat. He knows that this government had a heavensent opportunity this year to come close to balancing our international payments. He knows this sale will not only be for this crop year, but will continue in part for next year as well. He knows these markets are going to continue, and we must not endanger them because this very precarious position we have had with regard to our balance of payments for the last 10 or 15 years can only be met by expanding our exports and, as the minister himself has said on other occasions, by producing more in Canada. It was a heaven-sent opportunity to help the Minister of Finance, and because of the bungling and lack of cohesion in the thinking of the ministers over there, this sale is now in danger.
Our purpose in moving the adjournment of the house was not to interfere in any legal strike but to bring to the attention of the government that this was not a picayune question between the longshoremen in Montreal, Three Rivers and Quebec and the shipping companies; that this was something that hits at the whole economy of our country and is just as serious as was the railroad strike in 1950. The Leader of the Opposition divulged to the house today part of the record in this regard to indicate that this is not just a strike in the narrow sense of the word; that this is not a local strike but is a matter of national importance. Above all he laid before us something which I believe is a fact, that this strike in Montreal, Three Rivers and Quebec is a part of a struggle between the unions of Canada to preserve their own independence, and the desire of international unions to control labour unions in Canada. That I think is the essence of the problem. This connection between Hal Banks and the longshoremen, Hall and Hoffa is part of a struggle that the United States government as well as the Canadian government has to face up to at the earliest possible opportunity.
This is not just a question of the western farmers moving their grain. It is not a question of the eastern farmers getting enough grain to feed their livestock and poultry this year. It is a matter of great importance to our future as an independent and sovereign nation. Perhaps I am a little biased, but this government strikes me as one that is too fat to fight and too frightened to run. I do not try to go about this country causing difficulties in the movement of grain. I have tried to help, and all we get in return for trying are statements that they do not need advice. "We know everything. We have all the answers", has been their attitude; and today

we heard the most startling of pronouncements when the Secretary of State, when talking about Hal Banks, said he was not one to repudiate his friends. He does not have to go that far to show his loyalty to Hal Banks, because he is holding up the whole operation of this tremendous grain movement.
Nonsense.

Somebody says "Nonsense". You will find out how much nonsense it is when you go back and present your record on this to the country. Instead of 60 days of decision this period will become known as the Pearson program for panic. Two weeks ago today I made six proposals which I hoped the government would take into consideration, because they might have helped to move this grain. I did have some experience of difficulties in moving grain in 1961 but, I might say, on a much smaller scale than the tremendous difficulties which now face the government.
In the spring of 1961 it came to my knowledge that there was a possibility of a substantial sale of grain to China, not only for cash but a larger sale that we could arrange for credit. I asked those who are qualified to advise on these matters how much grain we could move through the four western ports. I was told, after due consideration had been given to my question, that the maximum amount of grain we could move through the four western ports was 15 million bushels a month. This was the advice of men who had spent their lives in the grain business. It was advice based on the experience of years in the business. Naturally, as a minister I am elected by the people not only to listen to the advice of my officials but to use the brains that God gave me. When you have an opportunity to sell grain and they tell you that all these difficulties are in the way, you try to find ways around them. So after asking a few questions as to what the difficulties were and finding out that, as is natural when so many organizations are concerned in the matter, each organization blames the other, I did what I thought was the natural thing to do: I called these 17 or 18 organizations to one meeting in Vancouver and put my problems before them.
I did not tell them to which country we were hoping to sell this grain, but I did say this could be done through the west coast ports if they could increase their capacity. Those same gentlemen, who had been telling me for a week before all the reasons for not being able to move this grain, settled this question. They sat down with their opposite numbers in the other groups, put their difficulties on the table, elected their own chairman, and within a week they came 28902-5-206i
Interim Supply
back with suggestions to improve the situation on the railways, grain handling, on the docks, on the prairies of Saskatchewan and so on. They were able to come back to me some weeks later and say, "We now have a capacity of 21 million bushels a month". That was an increase of 40 per cent. This was obtained by a group of men some of whom had told me there was no possibility of moving more than 15 million bushels a month. It was done by working together, and there was no extra capital cost required.
I want to emphasize that among the groups there was the longshoremen's union and the union for the terminal workers. Those labour men gave me their word that they would co-operate. They said they had in their contracts with their employers certain terms with regard to double and triple time, but they did not take advantage of those terms; and they offered to train new men to handle more grain. Those men kept their word, and when their contracts ran out last fall and they asked for a certain percentage wage increase, an increase which the unions at the head of the lakes had received when they asked for it, and they did not get it, they did not go on strike; they honoured their commitment to keep that grain moving because they had made a pledge to the minister, not to me personally but to the people of Canada that the grain would move forward to communist China.
In the light of that experience I suggested two weeks ago that there should be an immediate calling together of all the groups which deal with the movement of grain through the eastern route, through the St. Lawrence; that these groups should include the labour unions not only on the docks but those concerned with the terminals, and not only those at Three Rivers, Montreal, Quebec and Sorel but those in the Atlantic and the downstream ports. I suggested that the government should put before them the fact that in the national interest this was a great opportunity and they should consider these matters in the light of national responsibilities. I think if the minister had gone to the unions directly-because they are Canadians, they think as Canadians and they are not one bit different from the union men in Vancouver and given them an opportunity to see how they fit into the over-all picture, they would have made every sacrifice. The same holds true for the shipping companies.
I gave the minister this experience because I think it has a bearing. However, there was nothing done about this suggestion. There was a meeting between the government and the railways, and a good system of allocation of box-cars was worked out; but this should

Interim Supply
have been done with all the groups associated with the moving of grain to the St. Lawrence area.
I am sorry to say that the second suggestion I made has become a bit of a political football. For the last 40 years there has always been a disturbing thought in western Canada that there are interests opposed to the movement of grain through Churchill, and this disturbing thought never seems to get pushed far into the background.
1 have no doubt in my mind that the Canadian wheat board and the government officials must have told the Russians about the operation of Churchill. I am sure they must have; but unfortunately the Russians were not impressed sufficiently to want to change the shipping which they had already arranged. This was commercial shipping, and the situation as I understand it is that commercial shipping will only be using Churchill until October 20.
Western Canadians, rightly or wrongly, feel that the shipping period from Churchill can be extended beyond October 20. They know there is no difficulty with ice, even though they know that there is a little difficulty with slush along the docks. They know the federal government will also be willing to provide icebreakers and they should know- I hope most of them do-that it is because of the insurance regulations, which are not made in Canada, that ships stop coming into Churchill after October 20.
This is an outstanding opportunity to try and press forward with new ideas. The second suggestion I made two weeks ago was that the government-because the wheat board has nothing to do with this question of insurance on the oceans-should go to the Russians and say, "We know you are hauling most of this grain on commercial bottoms, but if you have any ships of your own that you can collect together and move into Churchill, we will guarantee they will not only get into the docks and be loaded but we will also guarantee they get out with the help of our icebreakers."
I know, from the records of ice in the north, that we could extend that shipping season a minimum of two weeks into November and, if one wanted to take a little bit of chance, right to the end of November and a little longer; but you have to give a guarantee that the ships will get out.
It may be that it was not in the Russians' interests to direct their own ships to Churchill, and if that is the case then a second proposal should be considered. They should have been told, "If you can persuade any shipping companies to bring their ships in there, we will not only guarantee to get them

out but we will pay the loss if any of them are damaged. That is how sure we are of that shipping route. In other words, it will not be necessary for them to worry about insurance from the London source."
I do not know if these two ideas would have been acceptable to the Russians, but I do want to know from the government if they were tried, because the minister's duty is not only to listen to the advice he is handed. A civil servant can only give advice within his experience, and no matter how dedicated and able he is, he only works within that limit; but the people elected as ministers can lift themselves above that level, and they will be judged on the success they have in the difficulties they meet, and not on their performance in coming into the house and reading out all the reports which the civil service gives them about this or that. They will be judged on their ability as ministers.
A third proposal I put forward at that time, two weeks ago, was that the government should go to the St. Lawrence seaway authority and ask them to extend the shipping season to a specified date. I have read in the press that the corporation has announced the shipping season will be extended, but that is completely useless. Men who control the movement of shipping on the ocean shipping lanes do not care for generalizations of that sort. They want to know if they go ahead and ship into the St. Lawrence, and maybe up to the head of the lakes, whether they can get their ships out again.
Shippers know there is no ice problem on the lakes and that it only occurs around the locks. I would say to the corporation, "We will come in and give you people our help to keep your locks free of ice, and we will guarantee those locks will be free of ice until such and such a date. Announce that date to the world and tell ships all over the world, 'if you come in we will guarantee you will get out' ",
That announcement has to be made, and there is no use in making a request to extend the shipping season a little bit. That is useless to the shipping people of the world unless there is a definite date guarantee.
The fourth suggestion I made deals with grain storage on the lower St. Lawrence. I mentioned in my introductory remarks that the economics of the grain market today suggest it is better to have grain-handling terminals on the lower part of the St. Lawrence where they have access to ocean shipping ways all during the year. There has been, of course, an enlargement of plants at Baie

Comeau and Quebec city, and there are requests in for other enlargements.
These matters were before me when I was minister and I recall the discussions we had to make sure-particularly if these terminals were being built by United States interests-that the interests of the Canadian producer in the west and the Canadian consumer in the east were protected in the licence issued for the new space to be set up. That is what we called the 40/60 formula, so that all that the American shippers could get in those terminals was the maximum of 40 per cent, on condition that they requested the board of grain commissioners to get it.
I now suggest that the board of grain commissioners should be asked to consult with the government and terminal shipping operators to make sure that every bushel of space available in those lower river terminals is reserved for Canadian wheat this winter. This is reasonable. All I am asking is that we exercise the rights we have under the licences. This is not only a matter for the producers of the country, and I am speaking now about all the terminals on the east coast, on Georgian bay and the St. Lawrence.
The question that has been in the back of my mind since the big Russian sale was announced, is that it is so easy for us, in our delight and general jubilation over the possibilities which this tremendous sale will have on the economy, to forget that there is a steadily growing market for coarse grains in eastern Canada, particularly for barley and low grades of wheat. This market will develop steadily until 1980, which is as far as we have projected, at which time it will be double what it is today.
The minister knows about this, and he has been making speeches to the farmers in western Canada telling them that they should take advantage of this opportunity. However, I am suggesting that he is not dealing with this in a practical manner. To make it practical you have to do several things.
I am speaking now about the eastern farmer and his need for grain. You have to guarantee him a stable supply, and you cannot do that, even by these new feed grain regulations brought in by the Minister of Agriculture, for the simple reason that the shippers make more money by hauling grain to the export markets, and they get more money out of storing that wheat for export than for storing domestic wheat.
My hon. friends who come from Quebec should be aware of these things because they are of more value to farmers in Quebec than the issuance of bogus money. You must give the eastern farmer feed grain at a price he knows is going to be stable. At present he does
Interim Supply
not know he can be assured of this, and once there is any hesitation in the flow of grain to the eastern market, the shippers know they can get more money moving grain for export and storing it for export.
Mr. Chairman, the following wire reached me at one o'clock today:
Following protest sent government on behalf domestic feeders: vigorously protest discrimination by Canadian wheat board not allowing domestic markets to purchase any feeding grades wheat except immediate use. Now price advanced five and one eighth cents since Monday representing along with increase in water freight rates hundreds of thousands of dollars extra cost to domestic feeders. Captive domestic market treated unfairly in relation to export sales. If CWB uncertain over available grades for feed some provision for purchase at price levels prevailing early September should have been made.
This was signed by Mr. W. D. Dernier of the Maritime Co-ops, and I am simply pointing out to the minister that I was not being facetious when I made these proposals. I know of the considerations and difficulties of moving feed grain from western Canada into the eastern market. I know the attitude of the buyers, that they do not want to take any loss; and I also know the attitude of the farmers down east who want to use this feed grain at a stable price. I suggest to the minister that if he goes into the reports available to him he will find the evidence of what I am talking about.
Something has to be done. There is no use in going out to the western farmers and telling them to reduce their acreage and cut production by 10 per cent, and I would remind the minister that after all this fanciful talk his colleague the Minister of Agriculture recently went to Moose Jaw and said, "Boys, don't squander your money." Hon. gentlemen opposite have separated the wheat board from the board of grain commissioners and from the Department of Agriculture. But it is necessary to work together with the Department of Transport; and the board of grain commissioners has to be brought in, because in addition to its other functions the board has to handle all these elevators, a job which is of vital importance. I know that hon. gentlemen over there have many competent men working for them. These men know what to do, so why not get them all together and tell them you want to make this move forward?
I wish, now, to make a number of other suggestions which may be of less importance individually but which, taken together, may add up to the moving of a number of millions of extra bushels. One of my first memories as minister was a problem we faced because shipping companies on the great lakes had transferred their tonnage to the hauling of iron ore for stockpiling in the United States

Interim Supply
because of an expected strike. I may say that the steel companies in the United States were not as negligent as this government has been; they planned ahead, and made arrangements for these ships to haul the iron into position.
I suggest that now we are in an emergency, even if this strike stops tomorrow, or one week or two weeks from today. We should ask the shipping companies to reciprocate and turn these iron ore bottoms over to us so as to help move the grain. A move of this kind cannot be made by the wheat board. This, ordinarily, is a commercial operation. But let us put on the pressure of the Canadian people and ask these companies to serve our nation, as Canadian companies operating in Canada, by transferring their ships to us for the hauling of grain for the balance of the season. This is one suggestion which should be tried out for size.
The sixth suggestion I have to make deals with floating storage. This is the phrase used to describe the practice of storing grain in ships which have tied up for the winter, usually at their home ports-Georgian bay ports and great lakes ports. I suggest the minister should approach these companies and say: We want to use your space for storage. You will be paid the full rates and you will not lose anything; but instead of your ships staying in their home ports we want them to move into the ice free area of the St. Lawrence. If this were done it might give us twenty to fifty million bushels of extra storage in export position without the necessity of moving grain by rail.
I wish to conclude by making a few observations of a general sort. I have already suggested that in my judgment, because of the great opportunities we now have, it would be of tremendous value to the economy if we could, to use the words of a United States presidential candidate, get the country moving forward again. Ministers have to use some initiative. I know many of them are former civil servants bound together by their habit of fitting into the lock step of the civil service. No matter how brilliant they may be it is hard for them to get out of that lock step; but I appeal to them to forget this attitude of being civil servants and show some initiative.

speechtext: He can carry on, of course, if he is given unanimous consent by the committee. Is that agreeable to the committee?
Agreed.

That is very kind of you, Mr. Chairman. I am almost finished.
The second suggestion of a general kind that I have to make is that all the ministers concerned should work together. I know how desirable this is from my own experience. It is necessary that the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Agriculture, besides, if you wish, the representative of eastern agriculture, who also has an important part to play, should come together, make a plan and go forward with it. If hon. gentlemen opposite rely on the advice of individual departments they will get lost in the morass. Bring these departments together and they will come up with answers; it cannot be done separately.
I have said all this, partly, I suppose, because I see such a wonderful opportunity and because I envy the opportunity which presents itself of doing something about it. But I am not over there on the treasury benches. The hon. gentleman and his colleagues are over there, and they have got to make these decisions. I know that what I call the Pearson plan for panic has been bothering them lately. I know that everything they have done has fallen flat on its face. But, I say to them: Do not let this one opportunity fall flat, please. Here is an opportunity for them to take their government out of its automatic shift type of attitude, where they shift every time there is opposition, and change it to one where they choose one gear and ride it for a while.
Even if it is low gear.

Do not let us have any more statements from the Minister of Labour saying he is keeping a careful watch on the situation. That is the same sort of statement as has been given for the last 30 years. We do not want a watch kept on this situation: We want some action.
My final advice, to the government, Mr. Chairman, is: For heaven's sake set a course and follow it.

Earlier in the day's sitting, when an attempt was made to adjourn the house I suggested that if the subject matter of that motion were left to discussion in the committee on interim supply the chances were there would be a wide variety of subjects discussed and that we would not be able to debate satisfactorily the topic which was of paramount importance. I think what has happened has proven the correctness of my contention. I think it is regrettable we did not have a debate on the particular subject of the longshoremen's strike, which is a matter of such great importance to the people of Canada. I do not wish to repeat what has already been said about how important it is, not only to the agricultural economy of western Canada but also to the entire economy

of this nation, that wheat should move in an uninterrupted flow from the prairies to the seaports and out into the markets of the world.
All Canadians were delighted at the agreements which were reached with communist China and the Soviet union. However, reaching these agreements and delivering the wheat are two different things and the task which now devolves upon the Canadian people and upon the Canadian government is to see that no obstacle is allowed to stand in the way of these wheat deliveries. That is why this strike is of such tremendous importance and why it could have such serious and far reaching consequences.
I rise for the purpose of pointing out to the government that this question did not arise overnight. The collective bargaining agreement which the longshoremen had with the shipping federation expired on December 31 last. It is customary to begin negotiations at least three months before a collective agreement expires. Yet when the agreement expired on December 31 nothing had been done to bring about an understanding. Negotiations dragged on until March, and in March the shipping companies made an offer which, as the Minister of Labour has pointed out, was accepted by the union executive but turned down by the membership. This was the offer of 12 cents an hour plus another four cents an hour fringe benefits, if I remember correctly. But the amazing thing is that nothing happened between that date in March and the setting up of the conciliation board a short time ago. About five months were lost and it was only when the membership of the union, or some of them at least, indulged in a wildcat strike which threatened to tie up shipping, and did for a day or two, that a conciliation board was established-the board whose findings were brought down at the end of last week.
Well, there is not much use crying over spilled milk, but I think the government should know that if there is any attempt to place blame they must assume quite a share of that blame for not stepping into this situation much sooner than they did. The Minister of Labour said this afternoon that the decision to strike was only taken last Sunday and he appointed a mediator on Wednesday. I am not complaining about that two or three day lapse. I am complaining about the months that went by last spring and last summer when absolutely nothing was done to bring this matter to a head and to try to mediate the dispute, and so have prevented the strike which has now broken out.
I should like to say that I hope the government will use all the influence it can to bring these two parties together. I hope that
Interim Supply
the government through their mediator will make the proposition to the men that if they will go back to work the government is prepared to set up another conciliation board and to let the decision of that board, if accepted by both contracting parties, be made retroactive. I think that under some such arrangement, by which the men are sure that delay does not involve loss of income, they might be prepared to go back to work. Certainly some concrete proposals should be put before these men and the companies as quickly as possible.
I think the government should know that parliament and the people of Canada are not in the mood to allow the dilly-dallying tactics of the companies to bring about a situation which could have very serious economic consequences for the people of Canada. I hope that the government and particularly the Minister of Labour will take notice that members of the house will be expecting not later than next Monday some report as to what type of proposals have been put before the men and the companies, and what response they have received.

Mr. Chairman, like many of my colleagues, I should like to comment on the present discussion concerning the $10 increase in old age pensions. First, I should like to assure the house as well as the people that I am giving my utmost support to this increase although I find it impossible to agree with the government as to the steps to be taken in order to secure the extra money required for such an increase.
The Liberal government's legislation to this effect seems most contradictory and it is rather hard for me to conceive that a government which pretends to protect the people's interest should once again be bold enough, more particularly in view of its notorious record in the field of taxation, including the 11 per cent sales tax, to secure, by means of a new tax, from the already thin budgets of private citizens, the capital required for the new legislation now under consideration.
Although they are attempting, by means of most disappointing economic theories, to prove that the private citizens' contributions will be tiny, not very large in the case of those whose income is low, the fact remains that private citizens pay proportionately more than the corporations and companies and that the burden lies once more upon the people's shoulders.
The Canadian corporations' income tax rate, including the provincial income tax and the old age security tax, is now set at 52 per cent in Ontario and Quebec and at about 50 per cent elsewhere in Canada. The Minister of Finance, Mr. Gordon, having been forced to

Interim Supply
retreat from the requirements put forth by Mr. Eric Kierans, the former president of the Montreal stock exchange, did not want to draw once more the financiers' ire and as the people do not constitute, as the companies, a monolithic financial power except on election day, it was easy, by juggling figures to impose upon them once more a new tax.
According to the government's policy, the companies or the corporations would be too poor to assume the cost of this new tax. The corporation income tax reaches 50 per cent from $35,000 on without any limit as to profits, while individuals have to pay from 50 to 80 per cent on taxable income of $25,000 and up, which affects them more directly. Moreover, individuals have to pay succession duties and are taxed at the source, while companies do not pay succession duties and otherwise, pay taxes only after taking into account depreciation, not to mention the many fiscal advantages which are allowed by legislation.
Moreover, our authorities seem to ignore, in their truly Liberal wisdom, that at least
2.400.000	taxpayers do not earn enough to pay income tax, and that 10 per cent only of the taxpayers, that is about 700,000, are earning more than $6,000.
It is then quite easy to realize that our population cannot assume this new tax. Would companies be able to pay it? Certainly. Here is the proof.
In the financial page of the newspaper Le Devoir of June 16 last, a notice shows that stock listed on local stock exchanges-about 730 corporations-were worth $54,837,791,829 at the end of April 1963, compared to $52,503,742,402 at the end of the previous month. Listed stocks had then increased by $2,334,049,427 during April 1963.
In 1962, on a gross national product of $41 billion, re-invested profits amounted to $10,400,000,000 for prosperous companies, while human beings and families did not have the bare necessities of life. Were you aware of that? Have you thought of that? Do you admit it?
Humans are more important than companies' stocks on the stock exchange of Montreal, Toronto or Vancouver. Humans should have more influence on your administration than stock listings.
In a country such as Canada, what is more important, prosperity and increase in value of stocks of 730 companies or the economic situation of 18,800,000 citizens? Would stock listings be more eloquent in the eyes of our governments than poverty and complaints of
6.700.000	children under 16 years old who do not have the bare necessities in 2,800,000 Canadian families?
[Mr. Latulippe.l
If we take a look at the assets of the 8 chartered banks in Canada, we realize that from 1930 to 1961, those assets have increased by $1,970,729,464 or 11 per cent. As of January 10, 1962, the Bank of Canada has issued $2,097,659,244, while the credit issued by the eight chartered banks was $17 billion, that is about eight times the actual money in circulation. So, it is obvious that the situation is rosy for the directors of the large financial companies of our country, but the government, blinded by figures and dual sets of books sees only one solution to the problem, to impose taxes upon the people who are already overburdened by the increasing tax load.
In 1962-63 for instance, for old age security purposes, the sales tax yielded $302.2 million, personal income tax $237.6 million, and corporation tax $115.3 million, that is a grand total of $691.1 million. This is to say that corporations pay 16.7 per cent of the total amount, individuals 39.6 per cent, or about 2J times as much as the corporations, and the sales tax absorbs 43.7 per cent of the cost, and who is paying the sales tax? The private citizens pay proportionately much more than corporations. Those figures are indisputable and they show that it is the private citizens who are footing the major part of the bill, not the corporations.
Now, when we analyse this government budget, either the whole budget or the interim budget that the Minister of Finance comes up with regularly, it is easy to see that the interests served are not always those of the citizens in general but of some privileged group. For instance, the estimates for 1963-64 provide for only 19.1 per cent to national health and welfare whereas the defence estimates represent 25.6 per cent. Instead of increasing the estimates of the Department of Public Works, which gets only 2.8 per cent, in order to create more jobs and so that a smaller number of Canadians may live on welfare, we increase the war expenditures. The cost of the service of the debt increases continually and this year it represents 13.5 per cent of the budget and no positive action is taken to change that situation.
We could easily raise family allowances to $30 a month, which would represent only 2 per cent of the gross national product, but no, family allowances remained unchanged, between $6 and $8 a month. From $11,400 million in 1945, the gross national product has reached $41 billion in 1963. Investments, which in 1945 were $1,284 million reached $8,770 million in 1960. Family allowances should have been raised in the same proportion to maintain the economic balance and

to prevent inflation and unemployment. But no.
If the government obstinately refuses to do something along that line, it should at least legislate a reduction in the exorbitant interest rates paid by our people. Because at the rate things are going, with the increasing burden put on the people with all those successive taxes, with this choking of family finances by the finance of great corporations and other companies, the day is coming when we too will have to deal with revolutions such as South America has known these last few days. Why, along with commissions on the civil service, education and public services, not create a monetary commission made up of experts in figures and people with a great sympathy for the poor who would be charged with the task of balancing need and goods, insuring a decent living for all, finding payment and credit conditions with foresight and honesty? If the whole country guarantees our money, would not the people be entitled to benefit from it, to establish the exchange rates which others can upset?
We of the Social Credit do not advocate taking money from those who have to give to those who have not. But since the government finds our economic and financial theories unapplicable and since our political philosophy does not agree with the present leaders of this country, since they obstinately refuse to use the Bank of Canada, we ask them at least to go and find the money where it is and to make the corporations pay proportionately as much as the individuals. We are definitely against any increase in taxation, we are for any social legislation which will alleviate hardships among the people, but not at the expense of the people.
The issuing of new money should be done not by the banks which charge interest, but through work projects, family allowances, pensions to the handicapped, etc., to give those people the means to buy a production which is going to waste. Then everybody will be able to eat one's fill, to produce according to his ability, to establish his family, and to enjoy a minimum of happiness on the road to his reward.
The nation should support itself before looking for foreign markets, before fighting its way in the field of foreign trade which creates depressions, privation, rivalry and war every 20 or 25 years. Let a national money more fairly distributed help us finance production and consumption and then we could import what we need. We would pay for our imports with our production or with that gold the Lord has placed in our soil and which brings no nourishment.
