This is a bill to change the title of the Department of State to "department of the secretary of state for federal-provincial relations" and to constitute a new department. See clause 2.
The bill also provides transfer to the new department of "any officer from elsewhere in the public service". See clause 3.
Furthermore, the bill vests the Secretary of State with new powers and duties. See clause 4.
I am of the opinion that this bill is a money bill and for that reason it cannot be introduced by a private member. It is inconceivable that the increased function of the department as suggested in the bill could be assumed without a vast expenditure of money. The officers transferred from other departments will have to be paid, probably at an increased rate of pay; they will have to be replaced in the departments from which they

Departvient of State Act have been transferred by new employees, thus creating a number of new employees.
On May 17, 1918, Mr. Speaker Rhodes decided that "A motion to amend a bill so as to provide for the appointment of additional government officials is out of order as it involves an increased grant of public money." (See Speaker's Decision-Beauchesne's third edition, 1943, at page 439).
On the same date the Speaker also ruled that "An amendment proposing to increase the membership of a government paid board involves an expenditure and cannot be moved by a private member." (See Beauchesne's third edition at page 475).
On March 2, 1927, Mr. Speaker Lemieux ruled that "A bill to create a new department of the government .... out of order because it was not introduced by a minister of the crown with the recommendation of the Governor General." (See Beauchesne's third edition at page 475).
On February 21, 1936, Mr. Speaker Cas-grain decided that "A bill providing for the transfer of a government service from one department to another involves the custody of public moneys and cannot be introduced by a private member." (See Beauchesne's third edition at page 478).
In the course of rendering the above decision the Speaker said, inter alia, "Another element which places this measure in the category of money bills is that the adoption of same would mean the transfer of the authority under which appropriated money is to be spent." And further: "When money is voted, the main conditions imposed on its expenditure are embodied in resolutions. All the circumstances concerning its destination form part of the appropriation with which they are considered and if any alteration is to be made it must be by the same process as the original resolution." And still further: ".... the circumstances under which an expenditure is to be made are indivisible from that expenditure. The choice of the minister responsible for paying out the money is a material condition of an appropriation, and in order to change it, the house would have to amend the principal clauses of a money bill."
To conclude with the words of Speaker Casgrain in this last decision:
I am therefore of the opinion that the proposed measure has all the earmarks of a money bill and cannot be introduced by a private member. I declare it out of order.
I regret that I must declare this bill out of order.

In my riding, there are 37,000 voters. They all belong to the working class, and they need to be defended. They sent me here to defend their interests and we shall defend those people in this noble chamber.

The day you will see a Social Credit government, you will see that legislation will not be discussed day after day under pretense that such is the tradition. We will know where we are going, we will come here with a precise and detailed program and in a jiffy we will see Canada on the road to progress again.
There will be no more strikes when you are in power.

The federal government cannot do without the provinces, but the provinces can do without the Canadian parliament, and they would be very happy about it.
Then, Mr. Chairman, should the house pretend that Social Crediters are unable to do anything whatsoever, are not sufficiently aware of procedure, it errs, for one of my colleagues shall also take the floor till six o'clock. And on Monday, we shall be able to pursue the debate on the subject of interim supply.
As to the recognition of the French fact, we have all found that-
Why soil it?

-in the house, there are more French since the Social Crediters came here. We work more for bilingualism, and we know how to put a French Canadian on the same footing as an English Canadian. For the time being, we do not intend to separate, we favour unity, understanding within the ten provinces of Canada with a view to a strong country, a country which should be able to govern itself, without having to bow before other countries stronger than ours.
We are blessed with an immense territory, big enough to encompass, within its borders, a population six or seven times larger than the present one. If, one day, the Canadian government thought of increasing our population by encouraging a higher birth rate, it would become evident that our land can feed many more people. Any measure which would tend to increase births, would give us a larger population. The day would then come when we, Canadians, could say: "As from now, we shall not be imposed on any longer." And we would become a truly independent country, with its own flag and its own national anthem.
For many years all we have been hearing in this house are promises to give Canada a flag. In fact, the man who is elected always has a flag design to submit within the next few years. And yet, after 97 years, we are still waiting for a flag, a national anthem of our own, as French Canadians, so that we would be recognized from one end of our
Interim Supply
country to the other and even throughout the world.
At the present time, what do you see on the ballot boxes when you cast your vote? "Dominion of Canada", that is colony of Canada.
That must change and it is high time it does. We count on the good will of the Liberals who have promised to adopt a flag, as well as a national anthem, within two years. Then the people will know what to do, if they fail to do so.
If it is decided to adopt a flag, I hope we will have enough imagination not to choose a ready-made one, but that we will take the time needed to study the design and that will truly represent French Canadians.
A few years ago, over one thousand flag designs were studied. One of them was selected, and I hope it will not be put aside, that it will be studied again, that its meaning to the people of Canada will be considered.
Mr. Chairman, this will conclude the few remarks I was pleased to make in this house at the beginning of this second part of the session that was adjourned at the beginning of August.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder what trick has made it possible to resume consideration of this interim supply motion at five o'clock when we were supposed to examine private members' business.
However, I am pleased to take the floor following my colleagues to discuss problems arising in my constituency, and there are many. That is why I want to submit them to the house, and particularly to the ministers present, as well as to the Canadian population.
Mr. Chairman, last year, I had the opportunity to speak a few times and to make these problems known. But because of the inefficiency of the government, who did not take some of these problems into consideration, I want to submit them once more to the house today.
The riding of Dorchester, one of the oldest on the south shore of the St. Lawrence river, comprises, so to speak, two classes of citizens. On one hand, you have farmers, on the other, lumbermen. And it is especially of those two classes of people that I wish to speak, since they appear to be the most dejected.
Mr. Chairman, there is no question of speaking of industry in my constituency, for it is small; wood cutting and agriculture are among the main industries we have.
Moreover, there are two classes of lumbermen. There are those in the upper part of the riding who work in the woods of Maine and New Hampshire, and those in the lower part, who work in Ontario or in the other provinces of Canada during the winter.

Interim Supply
Last year I had an opportunity to raise the problem of the lumberjacks who work in Maine and I notice this year that the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) who I must congratulate, at least tried to do something to reach an agreement with the state of Maine to bring those lumbermen under the unemployment insurance.
For 20 years, discussions have been going on with the state of Maine to solve that unemployment insurance problem and we do not seem any further ahead now than in 1944.
Mr. Chairman, in reply to a question from the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Dionne) the other day, the Minister of Labour stated that he went to Maine to take up the matter with American authorities. There seems to be some hope and I trust that before next spring our lumberjacks from Dorchester and the neighbouring ridings who work in those states will be entitled to unemployment insurance benefits, because, Mr. Chairman, those lumberjacks do not work all year round; they may work six or seven months a year, and that is why, we are asking for them the same rights as the other lumber workers and other workers in Canada enjoy, namely unemployment insurance benefits when they are out of work.
Mr. Chairman, the trade of the woodsmen is not a very safe one-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It is a very good trade.

It is a very good trade, as the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Pepin) has just pointed out. But it is also a hard one and I am proud to have in my riding many of those hard working people who put their hearts in their jobs and who are paying taxes to the Liberal government, because when a sales tax of 11 per cent was imposed-and the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska knows it-the lumberjacks were the first affected since this 11 per cent tax was imposed on their equipment.
That is why, Mr. Chairman, on behalf of those men I am asking the Liberal government to suppress the 11 per cent tax on wood cutting equipment. They are taxed enough; their income is not too high at the present time and this is why I feel that the federal government should take into consideration the lot of those men who are not making that much money.
And I hope that the Liberal government, which has been elected because it promised to increase everything but taxes, will show the same goodwill it had before the election of April 8 last, and will be pleased to abolish that 11 per cent sales tax on lumberjacks' implements.
Mr. Chairman, we also found a certain anomaly with regard to lumberjacks who are

not going to work in the state of Maine. Everybody knows that for about every trade, when necessary working implements have to be bought, like in the case of a garage keeper, a commercial traveller or any other trade, the cost of those instruments may be deducted from income tax. That is why I ask this government to take action so that our lumberjacks do not pay too much income tax, because they have to buy new implements every year and to travel to their work.
That is why I claim that they should be allowed to deduct the cost of those purchases and the travelling cost which they have to pay each week or every month to go to their work.
Mr. Chairman, I now want to deal with the problem of farmers in my riding.
Ten or 15 years ago those farmers were able to live on the land, but since then they are seen to abandon their farms more and more frequently. And as the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Perron) said this afternoon, everything seems to be organized in such a way that our farmers have to leave their farms.
I do not know whether I should call the existing practice patronage, but as the hon. member for Beauce said earlier today, what do we see? When a farmer makes a claim to benefit from some welfare plan, it is suggested to him, as a first condition, to leave his farm to go and live in the city. Today, everything of which we in Quebec were proud before, is being destroyed, which means that the family farm is now rejected.
But, Mr. Chairman, I can very well remember the attitude of the former hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Dumont) last year, when he was defending the right of our farmers to keep their family farm, which has always been a source of pride in Quebec. There were, last year, demands to the effect that the government should build storage space for feed grain in the east of the province of Quebec. This would have resulted in greatly lowering the price of grain and also enabled our farmers to make a little more profit, besides enabling them to remain and bring up their family on their own farm.
Mr. Chairman, it is a pity that such methods are used against our farmers today, to have them abandon their farms, which will enable the patronage people, probably Liberal, to buy those farms and turn them into a sort of collective farms.
Mr. Chairman, there is another point on which I want to draw the attention of the house. A few weeks ago the Minister of Labour designated some parts of the province of Quebec which might be helped financially by the federal government. Now, at that time, they forgot southern Quebec, that

is that part of the province situated south of the St. Lawrence; and yet that area would be fine for the setting up of new industries or manufactures of all kinds, because, as I just said, our farmers abandon their farms more and more, in brief they are unable to get a living out of those farms of which Canada was so proud in the past.
That is why I blame the Liberal government for overlooking the ridings of Beauce, Dorchester, Montmagny, and even the Gaspe peninsula. This last one was not considered because the Liberal member for the Gaspe peninsula had protested and because the Gaspe peninsula should not be considered as part of the country needing the assistance of a central Liberal government.
That is why I would ask also that all the ridings south of the St. Lawrence river be considered as needing federal assistance. Industries are needed there, not only to give work to labour, but also to prevent our young people from leaving the area and swelling the number of unemployed in the cities. Today, it seems that everything should be centered in towns, everything seems to encourage our young people to leave the country for the cities. The solution is not there. The solution consists in preventing our young people from leaving their home town. We can see the consequences of all that.
As a matter of fact, at every election, there are from 200 to 300 and even 500 fewer names on the voters' lists. And this is not due to a decrease in the birth rate, but to the fact that our people are no longer able to make a living in our parishes, in our respective counties, and must leave their homes for the cities where they swell the number of unemployed and small wage earners.
Mr. Chairman, I humbly ask the government to take due notice of the few remarks I have just made, because if the government was able to carry a bill in order to increase the indemnities of members of parliament, it could also pass a measure to increase family allowances, which are sorely needed today since the income in all classes of society is not sufficient to provide for the children's needs.
It is urged more and more that children should get an adequate education, that they be better educated in order to learn a trade and be in a position to work anywhere. This is the reason why I would again urge the government to keep one of its promises made in April, namely to increase family allowances, an excellent social measure. The government had not promised to increase the members' indemnities, yet that was the first legislation to be passed.
Interim Supply
But I urge the government to see that an increase in family allowances should not result in higher income tax. Private individuals are always the ones to pay, they are always singled out, but corporations, whichever they may be, are always favoured by the government. The poor and the lowly must always yield to the government. That is why, Mr. Chairman, as an excellent social measure, I request the immediate adoption this autumn of legislation providing an increase in family allowances. That will not only stimulate our country's economy but it will enable fathers to give a better education to their children.
Mr. Chairman, I should also like to speak against the patronage which is spreading throughout my riding just like in every other constituency. There has always been patronage since confederation because it has always been either Conservatives or Liberals who were in power.
As I was saying a while ago, the Liberal government or the Minister of Labour should sign an agreement with the state of Maine so that our lumberjacks who work there may get unemployment insurance benefits. The first advantage of this would be a reduction by half of the number of requests submitted for social assistance in my constituency. You know how social assistance requests work. If you belong to the Liberal party, everything is fine; there is no investigation and social assistance is granted without question. The organizing parties, the parish or the county chiefs have their say in such an organization. In the case of a Conservative, one is a little wary for this method has been largely put into practice by the Conservatives. But in the case of, let us say a private citizen, who will surely vote for Social Credit, there the trouble begins. An investigation is made, he is asked to give away all he has even to the last cent and once he is destitute, completely destitute, then he is given social assistance.
Mr. Chairman, that is how the two old line political parties have always treated the Canadian people, especially the people in the province of Quebec, as patronage in the province of Quebec is ten times worse than in Ottawa. As there is close relationship between the Ottawa and Quebec Liberals, you are aware that it is the same patronage that brews immense troubles for our Canadian families, especially those that are in need.
I should like to protest against abuses in the field of unemployment insurance. It seems that we have all kinds of legislation concerning unemployment insurance. We have unemployment insurance in our area, but one could say that there is a different act governing every unemployment insurance

Interim Supply
office. We submit a case to one unemployment insurance office and there they quote all sorts of acts. In another office, other acts are quoted which are almost in contradiction with what we were told in the first one.
I know that the laws were made for lawyers and by lawyers. One should absolutely be a lawyer to be a member in Ottawa. That is why the people were so much taken in, because we had in Ottawa representatives too far above the people and that is why the Canadian people, at the 1962 election, made no bones about returning to Ottawa men who were not floating in the clouds, but who had their feet on the ground, men who are able to walk along with every class of the society and who, most of the time, took into consideration the cases of the little people.
Mr. Chairman, I shall conclude my remarks now. Since there are only four minutes left before six o'clock-
That is long, four minutes.

Maybe the minister could
suggest a few matters I could discuss.
Just the same, I shall let some other colleagues have the floor until six o'clock so that we can keep on discussing how the government is going to present the interim supply bill now before us.
Since we know so well the Liberal party's underhanded tactics, we were not surprised to find out at five o'clock that there were not enough of us to continue the discussion on interim supply. It was thought that the Social Crediters had gone home. Social Crediters are courageous people, they keep their eyes open, and they decided to defeat the tricks of the Liberals. We have a sufficient quorum to carry on until six o'clock the debate on interim supply. As long as our party, the creditist group, is not recognized in this house, as long as we do not have our own seats, we shall be compelled to tell our hon. friends opposite, who sit on the treasury benches that we are happy to carry on with the discussion on interim supply so as to be able to explain the problems which beset our constituencies.
Mr. Chairman, I am happy to have the floor, for this allows me to put Dorchester county in the limelight. I have been able to ascertain by thumbing through Hansard that since 1867, the year of confederation, very seldom did the members for Dorchester set forth the claims of Quebecers, and more particularly of the electors of the various constituencies. We must indeed remember that the problems relating to woodsmen have not sprung up lately, but have always been with us. The state of Maine was also constituted years ago

and I am surprised that none of the members for Dorchester, either Conservatives or Liberals-indeed a Liberal represented the riding of Dorchester for quite a while-have risen and requested from the Canadian government that the lumbermen who work in the state of Maine be treated fairly.
Yet between 1940 and 1944, 47 American states agreed to negotiate with Canada and to enact legislation concerning the unemployment insurance benefits of Canadians from the English speaking provinces who work in the United States. At that time, there were 75 Tories and Whigs in the House of Commons and not one of them rose once to ask the same benefits for the people of Quebec who work in the states of Maine and New Hampshire. That is why I blame the federal government and all its followers. We should not have to blame again the Liberal government, for if it is well disposed toward those unemployed, it will take as soon as possible the necessary steps to confer with the American states in order that our lumbermen working in those states be entitled to unemployment insurance benefits.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Perhaps the house leader would like to give us his revised version of the order of business for next week.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think it would be very wise for me on this occasion to attempt to forecast the business very far ahead, because until interim supply has been granted it will of course not be possible, I am afraid, to do any other business at all. Therefore that will be the first item of business on Monday.
I would hope-as I think the vast majority of hon. members hope

that we might dispose of it fairly quickly on Monday after reflection over the week end. In that case I think we would have to reserve until Monday morning any indication of precisely what would be taken next. If circumstances made it otherwise possible, however, of course we would like to take the old age pension bill first of all. But in the light of the labour situation with which all hon. members are familiar, the situation both in Montreal and on the lakes, the government simply has, I think responsibly to reserve its judgment as to what should be taken after interim supply is concluded if, as I hope, it should be concluded.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may we take it for granted that on Monday morning at the latest the government will advise each of the parties what the plans are for that afternoon.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker, I will endeavour as early as possible on Monday to advise the representatives of the parties what would be taken after interim supply, if it should be concluded, as I hope it will be, on Monday.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Would the house leader definitely rule out a supply motion on Monday and Tuesday?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I am afraid we would be depriving hon. members opposite-even if the interim supply was disposed of in half an hour-of time to which they are traditionally entitled. I would not like to ask for that unless there was general agreement in the house that hon. members would be satisfied to do that. The government would like to have these supply motions because, as I have indicated very clearly, we must have five of them
Business of the House
in the next few weeks, and time marches on.
It was our hope originally, as I indicated to hon. members opposite, that we could take a supply motion on Monday, but several unexpected circumstances have arisen since I gave that indication and I do not think anyone would now like to predict what may happen tomorrow and Monday in the field which was the subject of discussion for a good part of today.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I appreciate the difficulties of the house leader. He will be reminded of my difficulties a year ago.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: My recollections are vivid.
It being five minutes after six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Monday, October 7, 1963
